content: The Sun that Illuminates the Profound Meaning of the Excellent Path for Travelling to Freedom, a Commentary on the Vajracchedikā.The Sun that Illuminates the Profound Meaning of the Excellent Path for Travelling to Freedom, a Commentary on the Vajracchedikā.Namo Mañjughoṣāya.I bow to the Muni, the lord of clouds, who rises in the vast, stainless sky of the Dharmakāya, who is adorned with the splendor of the thunderous sound of profound emptiness, and who releases the stream of rain of the two benefits upon the fields of those to be tamed.I respectfully bow to the feet of the noble Subhūti, who, through the display of the wheel of stability and the arhat, is skilled in asking about the profound meaning and providing all the answers, and who was prophesied as the supreme one free from afflictions.I bow to the successive spiritual mentors, such as Nāgārjuna, Āryadeva, Candrakīrti, and the second Victor, the father and sons of the Blo bzang tradition, who were prophesied by the Victorious One to explain the profound meaning.Here, I shall explain with faith, as best as I am able, a commentary on the three-hundred-verse Prajñāpāramitā, known as the Vajracchedikā.This text primarily focuses on explaining the meaning of selflessness and contains many repetitions.Although it is difficult to explain it exactly as it is, since there are no Tibetan commentaries available—only Indian ones—I shall explain it according to the capacity of my own intellect.This has three parts: the preliminaries, the actual body of the text, and the concluding sequence.The first part has three sections: identifying the title and the translation, the translator's homage, and the introduction.The first section is as follows: In the Indian language, it is *Ārya-vajra-cchedikā-prajñā-pāramitā-nāma-mahāyāna-sūtra*, and so forth. When translated into the Tibetan language, *Ārya* means "noble," *vajra* means "diamond," *cchedikā* means "cutter," *prajñā* means "wisdom," *pāra* means "the other shore," *itā* means "gone," *nāma* means "called," *mahā* means "great," *yāna* means "vehicle," and *sūtra* means "sūtra." Regarding the appearance of *pāramitā* here, it is because the *am* of the second case was placed between *pāra* and *itā*, the *i* was removed, and the *ma* was joined to the *i*, resulting in *mitā*. The explanation of the meaning of this title is as follows: Just as the diamond in the hand of Indra cannot be destroyed by other external objects, and just as it is capable of reducing to dust any object, such as a rock, that it strikes, so too the wisdom of realizing emptiness—the *prajñāpāramitā* which is the subject matter of this text—cannot be harmed by adverse factors, and it has the meaning of cutting off all afflictions and suffering from the root.The second section, the meaning of the translator's homage, is easy to understand.The third section, the introduction, is as follows: "Thus have I heard at one time, the Blessed One was dwelling in Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the park of Anāthapiṇḍada, together with a great community of monks, twelve hundred and fifty śrāvakas, and a great number of bodhisattvas." Regarding this, there were six great cities in India, such as Śrāvastī; this Śrāvastī belonged to the domain of King Prasenajit, and there was a magnificent pleasure grove there with excellent land called the Jeta Grove. Some time after the Blessed One had attained enlightenment, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada wished to build a great and excellent monastery as a permanent residence for the Blessed One and his retinue. He gave Prince Jeta many thousands of gold coins to cover the entire grove and purchased that Jeta Grove. Prince Jeta also offered a piece of land near the gatehouse to the Blessed One. In that grove, Anāthapiṇḍada, with the assistance of Śāriputra, had a supreme park built by divine and human craftsmen. When it was finished, the Blessed One, knowing the intention of Jeta, named the monastery accordingly.Anāthapiṇḍada was a holy, great being who intentionally took rebirth for the sake of the patrons who demonstrate the ability to see, freely take, and enjoy the treasures of precious substances located within water and under the earth. Then, for the sake of those to be tamed, the Blessed One put on his three Dharma robes in the morning, took up his alms bowl, and set out specifically for the great city of Śrāvastī for the sake of alms. After collecting alms, he returned and performed the activity of consuming his meal.Having abandoned the consumption of later meals or alms-food in the afternoon, he set aside his alms bowl and the like, washed his feet, and cooled himself; then, having arranged his seat, he sat down in the cross-legged position, straightened his body, and remained with his mindfulness manifest, knowing that this text would be taught. The Blessed One’s going for alms is not for the sake of his own need to consume alms-food, but for the sake of accumulating merit for those to be tamed and for teaching the Dharma and so forth. It is explained in the Suvarṇaprabhāsa that it is impossible for hunger and thirst to arise in a Buddha, and even if he were to consume food, since he has mastery over the wisdom of the Akāśagarbha, it is impossible for him to lack provisions; he is able to transform earth, stones, and the like into gold, silver, and precious substances, and he can transform those—as well as inferior food—into food possessing a hundred flavors, and whatever kind of poor food it may be, when it is taken into the mouth of a Buddha, it becomes food such that its supreme flavor is not experienced by others, as the Abhisamayālaṃkāra states: "In this, that which is not delicious appears as the supreme flavor," which is the meaning of that statement. In the past, when the Teacher demonstrated the manner of having to consume barley intended for horse fodder for three months, Ānanda thought to himself that although the Teacher was born into a royal lineage, the time had come for him to consume horse fodder, and as he felt saddened, the Teacher took a single grain of barley from his mouth and said, "Eat this," and when he gave it and Ānanda ate it, he was satisfied, and from then on, for seven days and nights, he did not experience the perception of needing to consume food, which is how it was. It is explained in the Suvarṇaprabhāsa that although it appears that the Teacher engages in taking and consuming alms, in reality, there is no consumption, and there is neither excrement nor urine, and in the Acintyaguhyanirdeśa-sūtra, it is explained that the body of the Tathāgata is like a golden statue, and that the body is devoid of internal emptiness, stomach, intestines, and so forth, which is how it stands in reality.Then, a great number of monks arrived in the presence of the Tathāgata, and having arrived, they circumambulated him three times and sat down to one side.Furthermore, at that time, the Sthavira Subhūti was also present, having joined that very assembly.The second part, the explanation of the actual meaning of the text, has two sections: first, the manner of the inquiry, and second, the explanation of the responses to it in sequence.The first is: Then, the venerable Subhūti rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One in this way.Then, to summarize the meaning: "Blessed One, you have performed supreme and excellent deeds to benefit the great bodhisattvas by means of the Dharma, and you have entrusted them with the three supreme types of entrustment—the entrustment of the spiritual mentor, the entrustment of the Dharma, and the entrustment of the command—so, Blessed One, it is wonderful," and so on, he said. Regarding this, the entrustment of the spiritual mentor is the entrustment to a virtuous friend; the entrustment of the Dharma is causing them to benefit others through that; and the entrustment of the command is the entrustment saying, "You bodhisattvas must benefit sentient beings," which is the intention of the master Kamalaśīla.The actual manner of the inquiry is that he asked three points: "Blessed One, how should one who has truly entered the bodhisattva vehicle abide, how should one practice, and how should one fully control the mind?" Regarding the second, the responses:The Blessed One was pleased by Subhūti’s inquiry in that manner, and having granted his approval and confirmed that it was so, the Tathāgata accepted the task of benefiting the bodhisattvas and entrusting them with the teachings.For that reason, he said, "Listen well and bear it in mind without forgetting, and I shall explain to you the three points you asked about earlier, such as how one should abide." In response, Subhūti replied, "Blessed One, so be it," and listened according to the Blessed One’s instruction, and the Blessed One spoke to Subhūti as follows. Although Subhūti merely assumed the guise of a śrāvaka, in reality he appears as an emanation of Mañjuśrī, and when the Teacher taught the Prajñāpāramitā, he appointed Subhūti as the first to teach the Mother sūtras, which is a matter of great significance. Regarding the summary of the text, the master Kamalaśīla explains eighteen points, beginning with the generation of bodhicitta, the application to the pāramitās, and the aspiration to attain the rūpakāya, up to the point of being fully sought by the Buddha; he explains the first sixteen in connection with the bhūmis of the path of aspiration, the next one with the bhūmi of pure superior intention, and the eighteenth with the bhūmi of a Buddha.Wishing to explain this briefly, the first point is the generation of bodhicitta: Subhūti, when one who has entered the bodhisattva vehicle first generates the mind, one should think as follows: I shall lead all those immeasurable and countless sentient beings—who, by way of their mode of birth, are gathered into the category of sentient beings—into the realm of non-abiding nirvāṇa, where there is no remainder of the aggregates of the two obscurations and suffering, whether they are those born from eggs, or likewise those born from a womb, from warmth and moisture, or miraculously; those sentient beings with form existing in the desire and form realms, those without form existing in the formless realm, sentient beings with perception other than those of the Akaniṣṭha and the peak of existence, sentient beings without perception who are a portion of the Akaniṣṭha, and sentient beings born in the peak of existence who are not without coarse perception nor without subtle perception; in short, all those who are designated by the name "sentient being" to the extent of the realm of sentient beings. To summarize the meaning, this is generating the mind for the sake of attaining the essence of the Buddha’s dharmakāya, the non-abiding nirvāṇa, for all those sentient beings. This is the newly generated mind that desires to lead all sentient beings to ultimate nirvāṇa, having been preceded by great compassion that wishes to protect them from the various three types of suffering, and if it is a mind that has already been generated, it is the act of clarifying and increasing that generation.Among the four modes of birth, egg-born beings include humans, nāgas, birds, and so forth, while womb-born beings include humans, animals, and hungry ghosts. Regarding heat-born beings, although there are many external objects such as crops, among humans there are cases like the king born from the crown of the head, and generally, insects born during the summer season. Miraculous birth includes the beings of the first aeon, gods, hell-beings, intermediate state beings, and also demigods and animals. Regarding egg-born humans, it is as explained in the account of the laywoman Sāgama during the time of the Teacher, where many eggs and subsequently many children emerged from her. The aforementioned is the manner of generating the conventional awakening mind, and this has two types: the aspirational mind and the engaging mind, which are considered to primarily refer to the stages of the path of accumulation and the path of preparation. For the characteristics of the generation of the awakening mind to be fully complete, it is not sufficient to merely desire to establish others in Buddhahood; one must also necessarily desire to attain Buddhahood oneself. Therefore, Maitreya stated, "The generation of the mind is the desire for perfect, complete enlightenment for the sake of others," explaining that "for the sake of others" means the desire to establish others in nirvāṇa, and "desire for perfect enlightenment" means that one must also have the desire to attain perfect enlightenment for oneself.In order to demonstrate that the generation of bodhicitta must be seized by the view that realizes selflessness, one should generate bodhicitta with the thought: "I desire to establish countless sentient beings in non-abiding nirvāṇa, and even after having established them, in the ultimate sense, there is no sentient being whatsoever that attains nirvāṇa." Here, the term "nirvāṇa" (mya ngan las 'das) appears; "mya ngan" refers to the two types of obscurations (kleśa and jñeya) and suffering, and "das" (having passed beyond) refers to nirvāṇa, which is the state of being liberated or having passed beyond those obscurations and suffering. Therefore, the term "das" also carries the meaning of both nirvāṇa and the act of establishing [beings] therein. This text demonstrates a state for ordinary beings that is in accordance with ultimate bodhicitta, and it also demonstrates actual ultimate bodhicitta, which exists only in the āryas.The master Kamalaśīla explains many aspects of the view in this context, and although it is important because the subsequent sections of this text are intended to facilitate the understanding of the meaning taught in connection with the view of emptiness, I will summarize and provide only a brief illustration for fear of becoming too lengthy. All phenomena of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are posited as existing merely conventionally, but when analyzed by the reasoning that investigates the ultimate, they cannot withstand such analysis and the object of imputation is not found; since it is easy to negate the object of negation once it is identified, I will first state what the object of negation is like, and although there are many ways of asserting the object of negation in general, here it will be explained according to the system of the Prāsaṅgika-Madhyamaka. As it is said in the sūtra, "They are posited by the power of conceptual thought," and in the commentary to the Catuḥśataka, "By the mere existence of conceptual thought, existence [is posited]," and so forth, and in the Rjes dgongs pa rab gsal, "It is taught that phenomena are posited by the power of conceptual thought," and as it is said that there are many teachings that all phenomena are merely imputed by conceptual thought and posited by the power of conceptual thought, the example of all phenomena being imputed by conceptual thought is this: when a variegated rope is situated in a place where the object is not clear, the thought arises in some people that "this is a snake." At that time, although none of the collection or parts of that rope are a snake, the snake that is thought of as "this is a snake" appears merely as an imputation by conceptual thought.In the same way, although the thought "I am" arises in dependence upon these aggregates, there is no collection, continuum, or part of the aggregates that can be established as the basis for the designation of "I," nor can any other entity that is essentially distinct from the aggregates be grasped as the basis for the designation of "I"; therefore, that "I" is merely designated in dependence upon the aggregates and does not exist by way of its own essence. In this regard, the *Āryaratnāvalī* states: "The person is not earth, not water, not fire, not wind, not space, and not consciousness; if it is not all of these, what person is there other than that?" By saying "not earth" through "not consciousness," it negates that the individual parts of the six elements of a person are the person, and by saying "not all," it negates that the collection of the six elements is established as the self of a person, while the final line negates a self that is essentially distinct from the elements. If one asks how, then, the person or *pudgala* is established, the same text states: "Because a person is a composite of the six elements, they are not truly existent; just so, because each element is also a composite, it is not truly existent." By that reasoning, the person is merely designated upon the collection of their own six elements and is not truly established. It is thus shown that, in the same way, the elements themselves are also not truly established because they are designated in dependence upon the collection of their own respective parts.In the same way, one should connect the idea that all phenomena, such as the aggregates, are also designated in dependence upon their respective parts and collections, and therefore do not exist independently. One’s own form aggregate is designated in dependence upon the five limbs and so forth; the limbs themselves are also designated in dependence upon the whole body and their own constituent parts; secondary limbs, such as fingers, are also designated in dependence upon their own whole and their parts; a vase is designated in dependence upon its own rim, base, belly, and so forth; and the rim, base, and so forth are also designated in dependence upon their own parts and the whole vase; this applies to all things possessing form. Consciousnesses are also designated in dependence upon prior and subsequent moments and their objects, and the unconditioned are also designated in dependence upon their respective bases of designation; this has been explained in detail elsewhere. Therefore, since there are no phenomena that do not arise in dependence and are not designated in dependence, that which exists without being designated in dependence is the limit of the object of negation for the exhaustive analysis of what is to be negated. As it is said in the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā: "Because there is no phenomenon whatsoever that does not arise in dependence, therefore there is no phenomenon whatsoever that is not empty." In short, when one searches for the referent of the designation of a self or person, it is not found, yet conventionally, like illusions and emanations, actions and their effects are tenable; it is the same for all phenomena, as it is said in the Samādhirāja-sūtra: "Know all sentient beings to be like the self.""Know all phenomena to be just as all sentient beings are," and from the Samādhirāja-sūtra it is also said: "Just as you have understood the perception of a self, apply that same understanding to all things with your intellect." Similarly, intending that one must understand that phenomena such as generosity exist only as mere nominal designations and are empty of intrinsic nature, it is said that one should practice generosity without abiding in any object whatsoever. This crucial point must be understood, for as long as one is not liberated from being bound by the grasping at true existence and has not realized the meaning of emptiness, one cannot attain liberation even if one is directly cared for by a Tathāgata; as the protector Nāgārjuna said: "Those who do not know emptiness are not established in liberation; those deluded ones will wander in the prison of existence of the six realms," and Āryadeva also stated that there is no liberation for those who have the perception of intrinsic existence, and there are many other such statements.As for what follows, regarding the reason why one must generate the mind with the understanding that no sentient being that is truly established attains nirvāṇa, why is that? Having addressed Subhūti, it is said that if any bodhisattva entertains the perception of sentient beings as being truly established as sentient beings, that bodhisattva should not be called a bodhisattva who has realized selflessness.Why is that? If a bodhisattva entertains a perception of sentient beings as being truly established as sentient beings, or entertains a perception of a life-force, that is, a living being, or entertains a perception of a person as being truly established, and if such a grasping at truth arises and is engaged in, then it is not appropriate to call that person a bodhisattva who has realized the lack of truth. Regarding the statement in the *Madhyamakāvatāra* that if the ultimate generation of the mind of enlightenment has not arisen in one’s continuum, one is not called an ultimate bodhisattva, this means that if one has not experienced the direct realization of emptiness, one is not called an ultimate bodhisattva; however, here, the explanation is given from the perspective of bodhisattvas who are in the two paths of accumulation and preparation. The etymological meaning of "sentient being" refers to those who possess a mind that is constantly tormented in cyclic existence; "life-force" refers to that which persists for the duration of the completion of a shared karmic lifespan in this life; and "person" is expressed in terms of that which fills the continuum with inferior habitual tendencies and causes one to leak into cyclic existence. Although the term "self" does not appear here, it appears below, and "self" refers to the basis for the arising of the grasping at an "I," thinking "it is mine," as explained in the *Śikṣāsamuccaya-vṛtti*. Although these are synonyms for "person," it is not the case that if one is a person, one fulfills the aforementioned etymological meanings, and there is also a difference in the scope of "sentient being" and "person."As for the method of training in conduct after having generated the mind in that way, since it teaches training in the other pāramitās as well, beginning with generosity, the first is generosity: "Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should practice generosity without abiding in objects," and the "objects" here are the objects to be given; thus, it is to practice generosity without abiding in the three spheres—that object, the act of giving, and the one to whom it is given—through grasping at them as true. This is as stated in the *Byams smon*: "May I practice giving without stinginess, not abiding in any objects," and as stated in the lines, "By whom, what is given, and to whom it is given, how the generosity is not perceived," and as stated in the *dBu ma 'jug pa*: "Generosity is empty of the giver, the receiver, and the object given; this is called the supramundane pāramitā. That which gives rise to attachment to these three is taught as the mundane pāramitā." Thus, generosity that is embraced by the wisdom that directly realizes the three spheres of generosity as devoid of truth is the supramundane pāramitā of generosity, and generosity not embraced by that is explained as the mundane pāramitā; the former exists in the āryas and the latter in ordinary beings. If one has not entered the path, even if there is generosity, there is no pāramitā of generosity, and the same applies to the other five. The phrase "like striving in generosity" is explained as the meaning of "how one should abide," the phrase "not grasping at its three spheres as true" is explained as the meaning of "how one should practice," and the phrase "making the mind one-pointed in the wisdom that realizes them as devoid of truth" is explained as the meaning of "how one should fully hold the mind," and this should be applied to the other pāramitās as well.Not only regarding the three spheres of giving, but one should practice giving without abiding by clinging to the truth of any other thing whatsoever.To explain this by making some distinctions: it means that one should practice giving without abiding by clinging to the truth of form, sound, odor, taste, tactile objects, and phenomena. Form refers to external forms, the objects of eye-consciousness; sound is the object of the ear; odor is the object of the nose; taste is the object of the tongue; tactile objects are the objects of the body; and phenomena are the objects of the mind, which are all phenomena whatsoever that exist as they are and as many as they are. Subhūti, apart from the fact that all phenomena exist merely as nominal designations, because there is not even an atom of inherent existence, to grasp at them as inherently established is to cling to a perversion; therefore, a Bodhisattva should by no means abide in the perception of grasping at signs that cling to inherent establishment. Grasping at signs is a synonym for grasping at truth, and the faults of being bound by grasping at truth will be explained below through an analogy.Although great merit arises from giving and so forth that is bound by grasping at truth, it is certain that merit is exceptionally greater if one performs giving and so forth by way of being free from being bound by grasping at truth; as to why that is, Subhūti, the limit of the mass of merit of a Bodhisattva who gives a gift without abiding is not easy for others to grasp, because it is difficult.To provide an analogy for this: it is like how it is not easy to grasp the measure of the sky in the ten directions, such as the east; this summarizes the meaning of the analogy taught by the words "Subhūti, similarly," and so forth.From the accumulation of merit such as giving, the form body of the Buddha is accomplished, and the form body is adorned with the marks and signs.The words "Subhūti, what do you think?" mean: Subhūti, how do you think about this matter, that is, how do you consider it? Although the two types of form bodies of the Tathāgata are endowed with perfect marks and signs, do you think that one should view, that is, desire to see, the Tathāgata merely by the existence of those perfect marks and signs? When asked this, Subhūti replied, "Bhagavān, one should not view him in that way," and he explained the slight distinction: one should not view the Tathāgata merely by the existence of perfect marks and signs; and as to why that is, he replied that the perfect marks and signs of the form body that the Tathāgata has taught are taught as existing conventionally like an illusion, but not as existing in the ultimate sense.The marks and signs of the form body are a conventional, false state of affairs that have arisen from the gathering of conditions, like an image drawn by a painting, and are not of the nature of truth; to demonstrate this, the Bhagavān said to Subhūti, "To the extent that there are perfect marks, to that extent it is false." If one asks, then what is not false? To the extent that the perfect marks and signs are not truly existent, to that extent they are not false and are true; thus, one should view the Tathāgata as being without marks and signs that are truly established.This eliminates the two extremes regarding the form body: because the form body and its marks and signs exist in the manner of the emptiness of conventional falsity, it eliminates the extreme of denigration, and because it is taught that there are no truly established marks and signs, it eliminates the extreme of superimposition. The former of these indicates the form body, and the latter indicates the dharmakāya, as the svabhāvakāya is the most important.The question of whether there will be sentient beings in the future who will trust and have faith in this sūtra that explains the dharmakāya and rūpakāya is as follows: Subhūti says, "Bhagavān, in the final five hundred years of the future time, when the holy Dharma is about to be completely destroyed," and so forth; the meaning of the Bhagavān’s reply, "Subhūti, do not speak like that," is to say, "Do not doubt whether or not such individuals will appear in the future, and do not ask."Subhūti, even at the time when the holy Dharma is about to be destroyed in the future, great bodhisattvas who possess the higher training in discipline, who possess the qualities of the higher training in meditative concentration, and who possess the higher training in wisdom—that is, those who possess the three trainings—will certainly appear; and I know that those great bodhisattvas have not merely served and generated roots of virtue before a single buddha, but have served and generated roots of virtue before countless hundreds of thousands of buddhas. Regarding the expression "the final five hundred" in the Kāśī [sūtra], a collection of five hundreds is five hundred, and since it is renowned that the Bhagavān’s teaching will remain for five periods of five hundred years, the five periods of five hundred years mentioned means that the teaching will remain for two thousand five hundred years. There are many different ways of explaining the duration of the teaching in the sūtras and commentaries, and there are even explanations that the teaching of the Sage will remain for one thousand, two thousand, two thousand five hundred, or five thousand years, yet these intentions are not contradictory. The way they are not contradictory is that some refer to the time of fruition and practice, some refer to the time of the transmission, and it appears that others are based on the perspective of Āryadeśa. Such bodhisattvas are like the six ornaments of the world of Āryadeśa and the like, and in Tibet, they are like Sa-pan, Bu-tön, and the Lord and his spiritual sons.At that time, those sentient beings who, through hearing and contemplation, have gained and generated even a single moment of pure mind—let alone much faith—in such treatises that teach the prajñāpāramitā of the sūtras, are known and perceived by the Tathāgata from this very moment, and those sentient beings will generate and accumulate immeasurable heaps of merit. Knowing refers to intention, and perceiving refers to form and so forth.What is the reason for that? It is because those bodhisattvas will not allow the manifestation of the perception that grasps at a self, a sentient being, a life force, or a person as being truly existent. The meaning of the terms self, person, and so forth is as explained above; for instance, the thought "I am," which grasps at the existence of a self, is the perception of a self.Grasping at what is "mine" is the perception of a sentient being. Grasping at the duration of that very self for as long as it exists is the perception of a life force. Grasping at the repeated movement into various states of existence is the perception of a person; thus it is explained, and the meaning of grasping at what is "mine" is slightly different from the former. That such coarse perceptions do not manifest refers to the context of realizing selflessness.Not only do they not engage in such fixations on truth as a self and so forth, but they also do not engage in the perception of form and the like as being truly existent as phenomena, nor do they engage in the perception of them as being truly non-existent as phenomena; thus, they will not engage in either the presence or the absence of such perceptions.Alternatively, it may be explained as the meaning that the perception of fixation on truth does not manifest even regarding conventional phenomena such as form, nor regarding the fact that conventional phenomena are truly non-existent; the fault that arises if such perceptions were to manifest is connected to statements such as "if the perception of phenomena manifests, then..." and "if the perception of the selflessness of phenomena manifests, then..." and so forth.Furthermore, the statement "The Dharma should not be grasped wrongly, for even what is not-Dharma should not be grasped" means that the "Dharma" refers to the holy Dharma of the scriptures, which should not be grasped wrongly through fixation on truth, and "not-Dharma" refers to what is not the holy Dharma, such as the treatises of the non-Buddhists, which should not be grasped; according to this explanation, it appears that one must examine it.For that reason, the Tathāgata, having contemplated this method, stated that this enumeration of the scriptural Dharma is like a raft, and just as one knows that a raft is not needed once one has crossed to the other side of the water, those noble ones who have reached the end should abandon and discard even those phenomena that are like a collection of scriptures—the methods for attaining the result—at the time when the result is attained, so it goes without saying that one should abandon what is not the holy Dharma, taking that as the basis. This means that at the time when the result is attained, because the purpose has already been fulfilled, such scriptures are not needed for one's own benefit, and the meaning is that one is no longer dependent upon them.Furthermore, when the Blessed One asked Subhūti, "Do you think that there is any Dharma that the Tathāgata has perfectly realized as unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, or any Dharma that he has taught?" Subhūti replied, "As I understand and know the meaning of what the Blessed One has said, there is no Dharma whatsoever that has been perfectly realized or taught in the ultimate sense."The reason for this is: why is that? Although the Tathāgata has explained that he has personally manifested and perfectly realized awakening conventionally, or that he has taught the Dharma conventionally, in the ultimate sense there is no Dharma whatsoever that has been realized or taught by him, and because their reality of being empty of true existence—the dharmatā—is not something that can be grasped by a conventional mind that corresponds to the object, as it exists in the perspective of the noble ones' meditative equipoise, nor can it be expressed by words in the manner of conceptual proliferation; for they are not Dharma in the ultimate sense, and yet they are not non-existent, as they are not non-existent in the conventional sense, and that is the reason.As for the reason, why is that? It is requested that because noble beings have directly realized the unconditioned dharmatā, which is empty of inherent existence in all phenomena, they are distinguished and established as such. These points refer to the fact that, in the perspective of the noble ones' meditative equipoise, the wisdom is free from conceptual proliferation. While it must be accepted that Tathāgatas are enlightened conventionally, in the ultimate sense they are not enlightened, because, as stated above, the Tathāgata is nothing more than a designation dependent upon his own aggregates; apart from that, neither his individual stainless aggregates, nor their collection, nor anything else that is essentially different from them is the Tathāgata. As the protector Nāgārjuna stated in the twenty-second chapter of the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā: "The Tathāgata is not the aggregates, nor is he different from the aggregates; he is not in the aggregates, nor are the aggregates in him; the Tathāgata does not possess the aggregates. What, then, is the Tathāgata?" and also, "Without relying upon the aggregates, there is no Tathāgata whatsoever." Here, the first two lines of the text have been combined for the sake of clarity. Thus, although his becoming enlightened and his enlightenment exist conventionally, they do not exist by way of their own nature; they are merely indicative. The way in which his teaching of the Dharma also does not exist by way of its own nature is as stated in the Acintyaguhyanirdeśa-sūtra: "The Tathāgata has not taught even a single syllable.""He will not speak," the meaning of this is found in the twenty-fifth chapter of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*: "The pacification of conceptual proliferation is peace, and the pacification of all objective referents is peace; the Buddhas have not taught any dharma to anyone, anywhere." Following the commentary on this, when the Buddha, the Bhagavan, has passed into parinirvana, he abides in a manner that is the pacification of all conceptual proliferation and does not abide in signs, which is the essence of peace. At that time, because all objective referents of grasping at signs are pacified and unobserved, from that perspective, the Buddhas have not taught any dharma whatsoever, whether of the realm of gods or the realm of humans, that is either defiled or purified. If the Buddha has not taught any dharma to anyone, how can these various conventional expressions of the scriptures exist? The statement that "the Teacher has taught us the dharma" arises from the conceptualizations of the disciples themselves, who are like those dreaming while possessed by the sleep of ignorance. This is also stated in the *Ārya-gagana-gañja-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, and it is a point difficult to realize. As explained here, one should also understand the meaning of the statement below that "the Buddha has not taught the dharma." In short, by saying "there is no dharma," the extreme of permanence is refuted, and by saying "it is not that there is no dharma," the extreme of nihilism is refuted; thus, having abandoned the two extremes of superimposition and denial, the statement "noble beings" and so forth establishes that, conventionally, great noble beings realize the nature of conditioned phenomena and manifest parinirvana.Although all phenomena, such as the attainment of Buddhahood and the teaching of the Dharma, do not exist in terms of ultimate reality, they do exist conventionally, and thus great merit arises from the giving of gifts; yet, the Bhagavan shows that the merit of practicing the hearing, contemplation, and meditation of this Dharma is even greater, by saying to Subhūti, "What do you think, Subhūti? If a son or daughter of noble family were to..." as it is said in the Abhidharmakośa: "A thousand sets of the four continents, suns, moons, Mount Merus, desire-realm heavens, and Brahma worlds is asserted to be a first-order thousandfold world system; a thousand of those is a second-order intermediate world system; and a thousand of those is a third-order thousandfold world system."As it appears in that way, the Bhagavan asked whether, if this trichiliocosm world system were filled with the seven types of precious substances—namely gold, silver, crystal, vaiḍūrya, stone-essence, musāra-galva, and red pearls—and given to others as a gift, it would generate a great mass of merit; in response, Subhūti replied that it would generate a great mass of merit, but he also posited that such a mass of merit exists only conventionally, like a dream or an illusion, and that in terms of ultimate reality, that mass of merit does not exist as an established heap, yet conventionally the Tathāgata designates and speaks of it as a "mass of merit, a mass of merit." This teaches that although past white and black karma that has been performed and future karma that will be performed are non-existent because the past has ceased and the future has not yet arisen in the present, one must still accept that they exist in a general sense, and one must accept that the result arises from that [karma] being connected to the mind-stream of the agent, and so forth; this is a somewhat difficult point. The mention of a "verse" refers to the fact that although this is not a verse in the Tibetan language, it is intended that it can be arranged as a verse in the Sanskrit language. "Holding" refers to holding the words in mind, and it is also appropriate to apply it to having the book in hand, as well as reciting it; "correctly explaining" refers to speaking the words and explaining them well; and "teaching" refers to explaining the meaning well, and this is intended as the primary aspect.If one acts by upholding it in that way, a mass of merit that is immeasurably and infinitely vast will be generated from that.The reason is that the gift of Dharma is of far greater benefit than the gift of material things; furthermore, the enlightenment of the perfectly complete Buddha is obtained and arises from this prajñāpāramitā, which is the meaning expressed in this text as the realization of emptiness, because the Buddha Bhagavans themselves also arise from practicing this.Although it is like that conventionally, in the ultimate sense there is nothing to be attained, for the Tathāgata has taught that what are called the qualities of a Buddha—such as the ten powers of a Buddha—are nothing more than conventional designations, and in the ultimate sense they do not exist; however, it is said that one may conventionally designate those various qualities of a Buddha merely in terms of the relative.That even the noble Śrāvakas attain whatever fruit they attain only after realizing selflessness, and that it is impossible to attain it without realizing that, is taught when it is said: "Subhūti, does a Stream-enterer think, 'I have attained the fruit of a Stream-enterer,' while clinging to it as true?" to which Subhūti replied, "That is not so."The reason is that although a Stream-enterer does not in the ultimate sense enter into anything at all, they are called a Stream-enterer because they have entered into the stream of the path to liberation conventionally. In the ultimate sense, they have not entered into anything, and they do not grasp at forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and phenomena as truly existent.The great commentary of the followers cites this passage, stating that if a Stream-enterer grasps the attainer and the fruit to be attained as truly existent and thinks, "I have attained Stream-entry," that itself becomes their grasping at a self; thus, because it teaches that grasping at the person and the fruit as truly existent are both forms of grasping at a self, the first is grasping at the person as a self, and the second is grasping at phenomena as a self.The fact that a Stream-enterer does not grasp with the thought "I have attained the fruit" by holding it to be truly existent is intended to address the refutation of the object of grasping at true existence, and it is not taught that innate grasping is also absent. This is as stated in the instruction that one should understand the subsequent ones in the same way. The meaning is that it is taught that one must definitely realize emptiness in order to attain the fruit of the cessation of suffering, which is free from the four, such as the Stream-enterer; and it is explained that having realized the lack of true existence, one must refute the object of the grasping at true existence.Therefore, whether or not one has experienced the refutation of the object of grasping at true existence is established based on whether or not one has experienced the realization of the lack of true existence; for as long as one is engaged in investigating any basis as to whether it is truly established or not, one cannot transcend grasping at true existence, and as long as one cannot refute the object of grasping at true existence, it is established that one is bound by grasping at true existence. Similarly, this is as stated by applying it to the three of once-returner, non-returner, and arhat, and the meaning is as before. Since there are those entering and those abiding in the fruit for each of the four, such as the Stream-enterer, if separated individually there are eight types of persons, and if the pairs are combined, they become the four pairs of beings. Although there are many explanations of these four, to illustrate briefly: the fruit of the śramaṇa-hood of a Stream-enterer, which is the truth of cessation, is established by way of having abandoned the three fetters abandoned by seeing; thus, one who has attained such a fruit and abides in it is called one abiding in the fruit of a Stream-enterer, and one who strives and enters for the sake of attaining it is called one entering it, and the three fetters are the view of a transitory collection, grasping at morality and conduct as supreme, and afflicted doubt. Although there is innate grasping at a transitory collection, here it is the conceptually imputed one. The fruit of a once-returner is established by way of having abandoned the sixth of the desire-realm afflictions, and one who abides in that is one abiding in its fruit, while one who enters by striving for the sake of attaining it is one entering it.The fruit of a non-returner is established based on the abandonment of the ninth type of desire-realm affliction, and those who abide in that or have entered upon it for that sake are those abiding in the fruit and those entering upon it. The fruit of an arhat is established based on the abandonment of the ninth type of affliction of the peak of existence, and those who abide in that fruit or have entered upon it to attain it are those abiding in the arhat fruit and those entering upon it, which appears to be something that would require extensive explanation if detailed. The meaning of a once-returner is that one must still take birth in the desire realm one more time, whereas a non-returner is one who does not need to take that birth. Furthermore, the fruit of a once-returner is established by way of abandoning the three fetters and the five lower-part-concordant [afflictions], namely desire for the desire realm and malice, while the fruit of a non-returner is established by way of abandoning the desire for the two higher realms, as well as agitation, pride, and a portion of ignorance, and there are ways of establishing these. These are exclusively Śrāvakas; here, according to the Prāsaṅgika system, all are Āryas, whereas according to the Abhidharmasamuccaya system, although there are ordinary beings among those entering the stage of a stream-enterer, all others are Āryas. In short, those four, such as the stream-enterer, do not hold to the truth of the one who attains or the fruit to be attained, and although innate grasping at truth may exist, there is no refutation of the object of that grasping, because all of them have already realized emptiness beforehand.Then Subhūti said, "Although I am an Arhat who has conventionally abandoned the afflictions, I do not truly grasp at the thought that I am an Arhat; for if I were to grasp in that way, I would become afflicted and thus would not be an Arhat.""I am an Arhat, yet the Blessed One has conventionally prophesied that I, the son of noble family Subhūti, am the foremost of those who dwell without afflictions, but he does not prophesy that I dwell without afflictions because I dwell in anything in the ultimate sense, for in the ultimate sense, that which is to be dwelt in, the act of dwelling, and the dweller are not established at all," he explained, which accords with the Prāsaṅgika view that grasping at true existence is an affliction.Not only are there no objects to be attained, no means of attainment, and no attainers in the ultimate sense, but it is also taught that there is no dharma to be grasped in the ultimate sense; this is shown by the Blessed One asking Subhūti, "Do you think, Subhūti, that there is any dharma that the Tathāgata grasped from the Buddha Dīpaṃkara in the ultimate sense?" to which Subhūti replied, "That is not so." The reason the name of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara is specifically mentioned here is that when the Teacher was formerly the youth Dharmodgata, he attained the great patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena through the blessings of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, and when he manifested the eighth bhūmi, Dīpaṃkara prophesied, "In a future time, you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni," and this will be explained below in order to remember that kindness. Attaining the great patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena means that because one has abandoned the afflictions and attained mastery in familiarization with non-conceptual wisdom that directly realizes the entire reality of all phenomena being empty by nature, it is not only in the state of meditative equipoise, but also in the post-meditative state that all conditioned phenomena appear as nothing but empty, illusory things. Because one has attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena, one directly sees that all phenomena are devoid of truth, and because one sees that everything—what was prophesied, what is to be attained, and the attainment of Buddhahood—is also empty by nature, there is no attachment thinking that any truly established dharma was grasped from Dīpaṃkara.Furthermore, at the time of the prophecy, the Buddha who gives the prophecy does not exist, and even at the time when the person who received the prophecy attains buddhahood, that person does not exist; yet, in terms of conventional designation, the persons between the prophecy of attaining buddhahood and the attainment of buddhahood are a single continuum, and because there exists a general "I" that follows through all the "I"s of the past and future without distinguishing the "I"s of the different times, it is with this in mind that the prophecy is given, saying, "You shall become that Buddha in the future." For example, although the "I"s of past and future lives and the "I"s of the earlier and later parts of one's life are not this "I" of the present time, one is still able to make the conventional designation that "I did" what was done by them, and "I will do" what will be done by them. Likewise, when I say, "I will do this and that," such as building a house or making a hat, clothing, or shoes, even though the house and so forth do not exist at that time, I speak with the future occurrence in mind; thus, although they arise merely as conventional designations, they are not produced by way of their own nature. If they were produced by way of their own nature, one would have to accept that the house and so forth exist even at the time one thinks, "I will build a house," but they do not exist. With such things in mind, the *Questions of Anavatapta Sūtra* states: "Whatever is born from conditions is unborn; it does not have the nature of being born. Whatever depends on conditions is empty; whoever knows emptiness is conscientious." The reasonings proving the lack of true existence that were explained previously should also be applied here. If one understands well the manner in which results arise from causes yet are not produced by way of their own nature, one will understand how it is tenable to speak of actions and agents within the emptiness of inherent existence according to the Madhyamaka system, and one will also find the Madhyamaka path of the union of appearance and emptiness.The teaching that one must establish a pure buddhafield in which to attain buddhahood in order to attain it in that way is as follows: if the Blessed One says to Subhūti that any bodhisattva who thinks, "I shall establish the arrays of a buddhafield with a belief in their reality as an ultimate truth," that statement is a declaration of what is not true.The reason for this is that the perfect arrays of the buddhafield, which is the place of attaining buddhahood, are arrays that have arisen from the gathering of many causes and conditions and are like an illusion; the Tathāgata has taught that those arrays do not exist as an ultimate truth, yet they are called "arrays of a buddhafield" as a mere convention because they exist for the mind that has not investigated or analyzed them. It is not only the buddhafield; all arrays of the environment and its inhabitants are also imputed upon the gathering of many parts, just like a house and so forth. If one analyzes all of them through reasoning down to the level of infinitesimal particles, they become nothing at all, and this is merely an illustration.Therefore, when a bodhisattva is to establish the arrays of a buddhafield, he should generate the thought of awakening without dwelling in such a belief in their reality.One should generate the thought of awakening without dwelling in anything as an ultimate truth, and without dwelling in any phenomena such as form, sound, and so forth, with a belief in their reality.The teaching that not only the external arrays of a buddhafield, but also the arrays of the bodies of sentient beings who are the inhabitants, do not exist as an ultimate truth but are merely a gathering of conditions, is as follows: when Subhūti was asked, "Subhūti, if a person’s body were to become as large as the king of mountains, Mount Meru, would that body be large?" he replied that the body would be large; the Tathāgata taught that that body exists only as a mere convention, as a heap of many gathered parts, and that it does not exist as an entity or essence independent of those parts, yet in worldly convention, that body is called "large." Therefore, that conventional body, which is not established as a body in an ultimate sense, is called a "body." Using the example of a large body, one should apply this similarly to all large and small forms. What is taught in this way is the method of meditating on all the environment and its inhabitants as being empty by nature.Regarding the example for demonstrating the merit of meditating in that way, the Bhagavan asked Subhūti, "If there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, would the grains of sand in all those rivers be numerous?" In reply, he submitted, "If those Ganges Rivers themselves were numerous, it goes without saying that the grains of sand within them would be numerous; there is no need to speak of it." Then, the Bhagavan said to Subhūti, "You must generate the conviction, that is, the aspiration, and you must understand this meaning."When asked whether a man or a woman would generate much merit by filling as many world systems as there are grains of sand in those Ganges Rivers with the seven types of precious jewels, as previously explained, and offering them to the Tathāgatas, he replied that it would be extremely numerous. Regarding the term "Ganges River," there appear to be two ways of understanding it: one as the river Ganges that flows from Lake Anavatapta, and the other as the great ocean; regarding the "sand," there also appear to be two ways of understanding it: as the commonly known sand, and as the particles of water droplets.Regarding the statement that the merit of reading, listening to, and meditating on this text is exceptionally great, the phrase "at least" in the expression "by anyone who, from this Dharma discourse, at least..." does not mean the limit. The rest is as before.Furthermore, the passage beginning with "Subhūti" and so forth demonstrates the discourse, for not only do such benefits arise from reading and so on, but the region or place where this text is well read, its meaning taught, and it is put into practice becomes a support for the offerings of others; therefore, it goes without saying that a person who takes the words of this text to heart and upholds them, carries the volume, reads it, masters its meaning—that is, understands it—and properly attends to it through practice, will possess supreme wonder, for in that region the Teacher, the Buddha, or any venerable holy being resides.Then, when Subhūti asked, "What is the name of this text?", the Bhagavan replied, "The name of this text is the Perfection of Wisdom; you should hold it by that name," which means that because the Perfection of Wisdom, which is the intended meaning, is made the subject matter, the Teacher has designated the text, which is the expression, with the name of the subject matter. By this, the name "Perfection of Wisdom" is used to indicate and also reveal the other perfections.That which the Tathāgata has spoken of as the perfection of wisdom does not exist as a perfection of wisdom in the ultimate sense, and therefore it is designated as the perfection of wisdom in a conventional sense. All such explanations that something does not exist in the ultimate sense but exists in a conventional sense demonstrate the Middle Way path, which unites the two truths while abandoning the two extremes; this shows that being empty by nature and existing conventionally both converge upon the same basis at the same time. The meaning of the term "perfection" (pāramitā) is the act of crossing over to the other side of the ocean of cyclic existence, or the state of having already crossed over; according to the former, it exists on the path of learning, and the latter exists at the stage of a Buddha, being synonymous with omniscience. Regarding the mere expression "perfection of wisdom," there are many types, such as the perfection of wisdom of nature, of the text, of the path, and of the result, but although one must know these distinctions, they are not discussed here. In short, this perfection of wisdom, which is spoken of as the wisdom that realizes emptiness and is seized by the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta), is a special method that leads the first five perfections, such as the perfection of generosity, to the stage of a Buddha, as will be explained.Here, when it is explained that the Tathāgata spoke of "that which is called the perfection of wisdom," one might wonder if there are other phenomena that the Tathāgata has spoken of in the ultimate sense; to demonstrate that there are not, when asked if one thinks that any such phenomenon exists, Subhūti replied that none of the phenomena spoken of by the Tathāgata exist in the ultimate sense, which is similar to the explanation of the meaning of the Tathāgata’s previous statement that he had not taught any phenomena.Then, to demonstrate that neither atoms nor the world systems composed of atoms are established in the ultimate sense, the Bhagavan asked Subhūti if the number of earth particles in the three-thousandfold world system is great, and when he replied that they are great, the Tathāgata taught that those which are the subtle earth particles do not exist as established particles in the ultimate sense; because they do not exist in the ultimate sense but exist in a conventional sense, they are called earth particles.Therefore, because the Tathāgata has taught that whatever world system is composed of accumulated atoms is not established as a world system in the ultimate sense, it is for that reason called a world system in a conventional sense.A brief overview of the reasoning for why those things are not established in the ultimate sense is that world systems composed of atoms are merely designated upon the collection of atoms, and there is no world system existing separately from the individual atoms or their collection; for example, just as a vase is designated upon the collection of its rim, base, belly, and so forth. Does a single atom have six directions—four cardinal directions plus above and below—or not? If it does, then because it would be larger than its six directional parts, the meaning of an "atom" would be lost, and if it does not have six directions, then because it would lack the capacity to occupy space, it would follow that the atom is not a physical form and would also become non-existent. Therefore, because a single atom cannot exist independently and must depend upon being collected and aggregated with others, an atom is not established independently, and because that is not established, the coarse particles composed of them are also said not to be established independently. In short, it is explained that one should meditate on emptiness by realizing that an atom is not truly established as having the nature of a single entity, and a world system is not truly established as having the nature of a collection of many. The master Kamalaśīla explained that the "world system" in this context refers to the world of sentient beings, meaning the impure world system that serves as the basis for the dwelling of sentient beings.The statement that not only the world, but also the Buddha’s Form Body and its major and minor marks are not established in the ultimate sense, means that when the Bhagavan asked Subhūti whether one should view or grasp the Tathāgata merely as a collection of those thirty-two major marks of a great being, Subhūti replied that one should not. The reason is that those thirty-two major marks of a great being, the Buddha, which the Tathāgata has spoken of as existing conventionally, were taught as being without characteristics in the ultimate sense, thereby refuting the extreme of permanence through superimposition; and the statement that "therefore, they are conventionally called the major marks of a great being" refutes the extreme of nihilism through denigration, and this is similar in other cases as well. By indicating the major marks, the eighty minor marks are also indicated, because the minor marks are the retinue of the major marks. The thirty-two major marks are as taught in the Abhisamayālaṅkāra, such as "the marks of the wheels on the palms and soles, and the webbed feet," and the eighty minor marks are as taught by "the nails of the Sage are copper-colored," and so forth. If one sees that the two Form Bodies of the Buddha possess clear and perfect major and minor marks and thinks, out of an attachment to truth, that the Buddha is established merely by these major and minor marks, that is not the case, because the two types of Form Bodies of the Buddha are called Tathāgata by virtue of having realized the Dharmakāya, and not by virtue of merely having attained a body endowed with major and minor marks; as it is said in the Aṣṭasāhasrikā, "One is not counted as a Tathāgata by having attained a Form Body, but one is counted as a Tathāgata by having attained omniscience." Although seeing a Form Body adorned with major and minor marks and then bowing to it out of an attachment to truth is included in the accumulation of merit, which is a good path, it is nonetheless flawed by being bound by the apprehension of truth, as explained in the context of "Those who see me by form," and so forth; for the Abhisamayālaṅkāra also explains that there is the fault of attachment through an apprehension of truth in such cases, in the context of the passage "attachment to the Victor and so forth is subtle." In this context, the apprehension of truth must be considered as ignorance, and it is explained in many scriptures that when one is motivated by ignorance and accumulates virtuous karma, one attains the higher realms included in cyclic existence, and if one accumulates non-virtuous karma, one attains the body of a miserable realm. Based on this scripture, in this way, of the pure and impure...The teaching that knowing and meditating upon all phenomena as being empty by nature brings great benefit is as follows: the Tathāgata said to Subhūti that even if a person were to give away their own body as a gift as many times as there are grains of sand in the Gangā river, the merit gained by grasping even a four-line verse of this Dharma discourse, teaching it to others, and meditating upon it would be far greater. This also reflects the benefits mentioned by Ārya Deva, who said: "One who has little merit will not even feel doubt about this Dharma; yet, by merely feeling doubt, one will cause existence to crumble." However, for the sake of future disciples of lesser intellect who possess faith, and in order to generate enthusiasm for the benefits so that they may engage in the study and contemplation of the text, it is taught in the manner of praise that if one grasps and recites even a four-line verse, such vast benefits will arise. The actual underlying intention is that one will attain the perfection of such benefits through the prajñāpāramitā of the meaning taught in that way, rather than that one will attain the entirety of such benefits merely by reading the text. This principle should also be understood in other such contexts.When it was spoken in this way, Subhūti, having heard this profound Dharma, was overcome by the force of his wonder and shed tears from his eyes; then, having wiped away his tears, he said to the Blessed One that it is truly wonderful that this prajñāpāramitā Dharma has been spoken by all the Tathāgatas who have appeared and resided.The statement, "Subhūti, ever since I attained the wisdom of the Āryas, I have not heard this Dharma discourse, and furthermore, I have never heard it before," does not mean that Subhūti had never heard such things in the past, but rather it demonstrates that it is difficult for others to hear such a profound Dharma of prajñāpāramitā.Regarding the manner in which it is wonderful: those sentient beings who, upon hearing the words and meaning of this sūtra, generate a correct perception free from attachment to truth, are endowed with great wonder because they plant the imprints of liberation and grasp the great cause for attaining Buddhahood.What is explained as "correct perception" is so because it is devoid of the perception of attachment to truth; therefore, the Tathāgata has spoken of that perception which is free from attachment to truth and realizes the non-existence of truth as "correct perception.""Bhagavān, that I have generated conviction by contemplating and understanding the meaning of this Dharma discourse does not constitute a great wonder for me; however, those sentient beings in the future who generate conviction in the meaning of emptiness and take up this Dharma and so forth will be endowed with a supreme, great wonder." This manner is indeed wonderful, as the protector Nāgārjuna stated: "To understand that phenomena are empty, yet still rely upon actions and their results—this is more wonderful than wonderful, more marvelous than marvelous!" The meaning of the other parts has already been explained, and regarding the "questioning," if it is taken as "asking," it connects to asking about other meanings, whereas if it is taken as "writing," it connects to writing it down in letters; however, according to the *Madhyāntavibhāga*, which states, "writing the letters, making offerings, and giving," it is the latter. These texts demonstrate the manner of how one should abide, how one should practice, and how one should uphold this.For those sentient beings who, in the future time, engage with a text such as this through hearing, reflecting, and meditating, the coarse perception of a self of a person will not arise, and likewise, the various perceptions of attachment to the truth of a sentient being, a life force, and a person will not arise or be produced.The reason is that such perceptions of a self and so forth are engaged in a distorted manner toward the object of attachment, and thus, because they are devoid of all authentic perceptions, or because these perceptions are devoid of being established as perceptions in the ultimate sense, when this was asked, the Bhagavān said to Subhūti, "It is indeed so," and the reason is: in the future, when sentient beings hear the words and meaning of this sūtra being taught, they will not be frightened, terrified, or extremely alarmed by the thought that if all things are thus without truth, then actions, results, and so forth would be untenable and non-existent, and those who trust and generate conviction will be endowed with a supreme, great wonder. If things were established as true, they could not be transformed, and thus all actions and agents such as karma and its results would be untenable and impossible to posit, whereas the manner in which all actions, agents, and nirvāṇa are tenable when things are not true or not established by way of their own nature is as stated in the *Ratnāvalī* (or *Ratnāvalī-stotra*): "Because there is no reversal of inherent nature, if phenomena had any inherent nature, nirvāṇa would be impossible, and it is taught that there would be no reversal of all conceptual proliferation," and as stated: "Because they are empty by way of their own nature, it is not contradictory for actions and agents to be tenable, whereas when one sees them as the reverse of that, actions are not tenable in the empty."The reason for its being wonderful is that this supreme and excellent prajñāpāramitā, the scripture that teaches that all phenomena are not inherently established, is now spoken by me, the Tathāgata, because it was spoken by countless Buddhas, Bhagavans, in the past. This was spoken in order to establish it as a basis for confidence in the explanation given above that phenomena of cause and effect are devoid of inherent existence.For that reason, it is called the supreme prajñāpāramitā.Next, regarding the specific explanation of the perfection of patience: Subhūti, that which is called the perfection of patience is, in the ultimate sense, non-existent, and therefore one must not grasp at the three spheres—the one who practices patience, the manner or object of patience, and that toward which patience is directed—with an attachment to their truth. The reason is that, Subhūti, in the past, when the King of Kaliṅga, having developed a malicious suspicion that I was involved with his women, used a sword to sever my limbs, minor limbs, and fingers, at that time, I knew the three spheres of patience to be devoid of truth and practiced patience; thus, there did not arise in me the perception of a self, grasping at the conventional "I" as truly existing, nor did there arise the perception of a person, grasping at a person as truly existing. At that time, I had no such perception of true existence, yet it is not the case that I was without any other conventional perceptions, for I possessed the perception of accepting suffering, the perception of being unperturbed by harm, and the perception of certain conviction in the Dharma, which is realized as devoid of truth, he thought.The reason is that if, at that time, I had possessed a perception of a self as truly existing in the ultimate sense, such as thinking "I am," then at that time a perception of malevolence toward others would also have arisen, but because that did not arise, it is said.Furthermore, I know and perceive that when I was a sage called Kṣāntivādin for five hundred lifetimes in the past, at the time when my limbs and so forth were severed by others due to such circumstances, no perception of a self or the like arose. If one thinks, "If the 'I' at the time the limbs were severed is not the Teacher, and the Teacher is not that 'I' of that time, how is it consistent for the Teacher to speak of 'my' limbs?" it is true, but since a detailed answer to this would be lengthy, in summary, it refers to the same continuum, and the manner in which it is faultless has been explained somewhat above and will be explained further. That grasping at a self—thinking "I am"—leads to the arising of malevolence and so forth is as stated in the Pramāṇavārttika: "When there is a self, there is the cognition of an other. Through the division of self and other, grasping and aversion arise. From being thoroughly entangled with these, all faults come to be."Because I attained buddhahood through such power of patience, for that reason, bodhisattvas should thoroughly abandon such perception of a self and generate the mind toward unsurpassed awakening, causing it to flourish. Not only do they not abide in the three spheres of patience through clinging to truth, but they also do not abide in that way regarding form, sound, and so forth; they do not abide in any conventional phenomena through clinging to truth, and they should not abide through clinging to truth even in the ultimate, which is the absence of truth in conventional phenomena.The reason is that the objects of clinging and abiding, such as form and sound, do not abide ultimately, as they are not established.Therefore, the Tathāgata has said that a bodhisattva should practice generosity without abiding in anything ultimately, and it is intended that this be applied to ethical discipline and the others as well. A bodhisattva should thus completely relinquish generosity and observe ethical discipline and so forth in this manner of having no clinging to truth.Even that very perception of a "sentient being" as true is, in the ultimate sense, devoid of perception, and those sentient beings who are spoken of in conventional terms are themselves also not established by their own nature as sentient beings.The reason is that, Subhūti, the Tathāgata’s explanation of phenomena as being empty of truth is not spoken falsely, for the Tathāgata is one who speaks correctly without error, one who speaks of the truth that does not change into another state, and one who speaks of the nature of phenomena just as it is, and is not one who speaks falsely.Subhūti, the Tathāgata has said that among those phenomena that are to be attained, whether buddhahood or the teachings, there are no phenomena of ultimate truth that are established as true, nor are there any deceptive conventional phenomena that are established as true. Kamalaśīla explains that because conventional phenomena do not exist in the nature of the wisdom that investigates the ultimate, they appear as untrue and deceptive, and this text also eliminates the two extremes.To demonstrate that there is a difference in the activity of generosity and so forth depending on whether or not one has realized the lack of true existence, it is taught as follows: for example, just as a person endowed with sight who has entered into great darkness does not clearly see any object of form, in the same way, those bodhisattvas who have not directed their minds toward the lack of true existence and who, having fallen into the abyss of the view of intense attachment bound by the grasping at true existence, practice generosity, should be viewed as bodhisattvas who are like that example.Furthermore, just as when the night ends and the sun rises, a person endowed with sight sees various kinds of good and bad forms, in the same way, those bodhisattvas who do not fall into the entities bound by grasping at true existence and who practice generosity should be viewed as being like that example; thus, it is explained that generosity bound by grasping at true existence is like a person who has entered into darkness and cannot see forms, while generosity that realizes the lack of true existence is like a person with sight who sees forms. Furthermore, the five perfections such as generosity that are not seized by the wisdom realizing the lack of true existence are like the blind, and the perfection of wisdom that realizes the lack of true existence is like a sighted person leading the blind; as the *Saṃcayagāthā* states: "How could many millions of blind people, lacking a guide, know the path or enter the city? Without wisdom, these five perfections are sightless, and being without a guide, they are unable to touch enlightenment." Following this statement, it is taught that if those first five perfections are not seized by the perfection of wisdom that realizes the lack of true existence, they are like the sightless and cannot travel to the level of a buddha, whereas if they are seized, they are like the sighted and can travel there; connecting this to the previous point, it is said: "When one is thoroughly seized by wisdom, at that time one has found an eye and attained the name of this." The glorious Candrakīrti also states in the *Madhyamakāvatāra*: "Just as a single sighted person, by their own desire, easily leads a multitude of blind people to their destination, in the same way, here too, through wisdom, one takes up the qualities of the sighted and proceeds to the state of a conqueror."Then, the statement that the Tathāgata knows and sees from the present moment onwards whichever individuals will arise who hold, retain, and so forth, this text in the present and future times, and that all those beings will generate an immeasurable mass of merit, means that the Buddha, having taken those beings into his heart, generates enthusiasm by saying that their merit is great.Furthermore, it is said that if someone were to give away their body in the morning, in the evening, and throughout many aeons, sacrificing bodies as numerous as the grains of sand in the Gangā river, and if, compared to the benefit of that sacrifice, someone were to hear this text in its entirety, believe in it, and not abandon it with their mind, the mass of merit of that person would be greater than the former; so what need is there to mention that the merit would be even greater if one were to write this text down in letters and so forth? Moreover, from the act of receiving it up to the act of fully explaining it, each subsequent stage is of greater merit and benefit than the one preceding it.The praise is because the meaning of this discourse on the Dharma is profound and difficult to realize, and thus it is inconceivable and there is no other that is equal or comparable to it; one should know and understand that the ripened result of having heard, contemplated, and meditated upon this is also vast and inconceivable.This Dharma was not spoken primarily for the sake of those who aspire to the Lesser Vehicle, but rather the Tathāgata spoke it for the sake of the beings, the bodhisattvas, who have entered the path of the Great Vehicle, the supreme vehicle and the ultimate vehicle. The supreme vehicle and the ultimate vehicle are both synonyms for the Great Vehicle.Those sentient beings of the Great Vehicle who take up and hold this Dharma are known and seen by the Tathāgata from this very moment, and those sentient beings will possess a mass of merit that is immeasurable, inconceivable, incomparable, unfathomable, and boundless, and all those sentient beings will quickly attain the level of my, the Tathāgata’s, enlightenment, just as if it were placed in the palm of their hand.The reason is that those who aspire to the Lesser Vehicle are unable to listen to this profound discourse on the Dharma by way of hearing, contemplating, and meditating, because they view things with a belief in the reality of a self of a person, a sentient being, a life-force, and a person, and those who are like externalists who desire such things are unable to listen to or take up the words and meaning of this text, for they lack the basis or opportunity to do so, because such sentient beings do not desire the meaning of selflessness.Furthermore, any place where this sūtra is taught becomes a place worthy of being offered to, prostrated to, and circumambulated by the sentient beings of the world, including gods, humans, and asuras, and that place becomes like a stūpa. This is similar to what is stated in the Abhisamayālaṃkāra, where it says, "The enlightenment is the object of veneration," and in the extensive, intermediate, and concise versions of the Mother sūtras and their commentaries, where it is said that the place where a Bodhisattva on the path of meditation dwells is a place of veneration by others, like a stūpa; primarily, however, this refers to the place where a person dwells in whose continuum the special prajñāpāramitā, which is the subject matter of this text, has arisen. Although something similar to this was mentioned above, that was done with respect to different bases.Furthermore, Subhūti, it is possible that those sentient beings who uphold, retain, and so forth, this sūtra and put its meaning into practice might be tormented by various illnesses, disputes, accusations, and bindings and beatings, and might experience extreme suffering, yet this is not a great fault. Why is that? Because the results of all the non-virtuous actions that those sentient beings committed in this life and in previous lives, which would have caused them to be reborn in the three lower realms, will ripen at the beginning of this very life, and by the power of being tormented by that suffering, all those non-virtuous actions from previous lives will be exhausted and purified, and they will also quickly attain the enlightenment of a Buddha.
