If it is said that by the power of practicing the antidote of striving in prajñāpāramitā, one destroys the root of all non-virtuous actions—self-grasping—and attains liberation and omniscience, then it goes without saying that one destroys the actions that would cause rebirth in the lower realms. This manner is explained in the Tarkajvālā and other texts, and the Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra also states: "Even if there is non-virtue that would cause rebirth in the lower realms, it is purified merely by a headache." For example, just as a seed that has been planted will not sprout if it is completely devoid of water, fertilizer, warmth, and moisture, if one is able to abandon self-grasping, then no matter what karma has been accumulated, it cannot produce its maturation because the cooperative condition of the afflictions is absent, as stated in the Pramāṇavārttika: "Karma that has transcended the craving for existence is incapable of projecting another life, because its cooperative conditions have been exhausted."Subhūti, I have realized and known that in the past, during an immeasurable and even more immeasurable number of aeons, and even before the time of the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, there appeared eighty-four quadrillion Buddhas, all of whom I worshipped, served, and pleased, never causing them dissatisfaction or distress. Between the merit I gained from doing so and the merit gained in the final period of the five hundred years by writing down this sūtra and so forth, this latter mass of merit is greater; the former mass of merit does not approach even a hundredth part of it, nor does it come close to a thousandth part, a hundred-thousandth part, or any number, measure, calculation, example, likeness, or cause, and it is unable to compete with it. Although all of these are examples, the parts differ in terms of their magnitude, the numbers differ in their quantity, the examples are not the same, the comparisons are unequal, the reasons are different, and the calculations cannot be counted as equivalent.If one were to clearly distinguish and state, "This is the kind of mass of merit that those who generate and uphold it will possess," beings with inferior intellects would not believe it, and, becoming confused and bewildered, their minds would be greatly disturbed.Although this dharma discourse is brief in its text, its meaning is vast and therefore inconceivable, and the result of ripening from practicing its meaning is also inconceivable. One should not understand the term "result of ripening" as referring only to the ripened result; it also includes the result concordant with the cause, the result of possession, the result of separation, and so forth. Something like this has appeared previously, but it was spoken with a view to different contexts.Furthermore, the Blessed One was asked by Subhūti, "How should one who has entered the path of the Bodhisattva abide?" and so forth. Although something like this occurred previously, it was in the context of the path of accumulation and the stage of aspiration; here, however, it is spoken with a view to the time when one is near to attaining the path of seeing and the time of having attained it, and the meaning is as explained before.It concludes by stating that there is no phenomenon whatsoever that is truly established as having entered the vehicle of the Bodhisattva.Furthermore, when Subhūti was asked, "Do you think, Subhūti, that there is any phenomenon that the Tathāgata attained in the presence of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara in the past, by which he became a Buddha?" Subhūti replied, "That does not exist," and the Blessed One confirmed it by saying, "That is so," in words, and "That is so," in meaning, for there is no such phenomenon whatsoever.If there were any such phenomenon, the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara would not have prophesied to me, "Young Brahmin, in a future time you shall be called the Buddha Śākyamuni," because there is no phenomenon whatsoever that is truly established as having attained perfect and complete buddhahood. At that time, the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara prophesied my awakening in that way. The manner in which those phenomena—by whom, what, and where something is prophesied—are merely nominal designations and names, and are not truly established, has already been explained above. It is taught in the sūtras that ninety-one aeons have passed since the Buddha Dīpaṃkara appeared, and the annotations to the *Sgron gsal*, the commentary on the *’Dus pa’i rtsa rgyud*, also state that the later Dīpaṃkara appeared ninety-one great aeons ago. At that time, when the teacher was a young Brahmin who had become a cloud of Dharma, that very Buddha placed his feet upon his body and blessed him, whereby he attained the great patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena and was prophesied to attain buddhahood. In general, there are three levels of attaining the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena: small, medium, and great; the small arises upon attaining the path of preparation, the medium upon the path of seeing, and the great upon attaining the state of an arhat, while in the context of the Great Vehicle, it is attained from the eighth stage onwards. To attain any of these three types of patient acceptance, one must realize that conditioned phenomena are by nature unarisen, and therefore one must definitely realize emptiness; for the medium and great levels, one must realize emptiness directly, and for the great level, one must also have abandoned the afflictions. Therefore, to be explicitly prophesied to attain buddhahood, one must have already realized emptiness; thus, a bodhisattva who is bound by the grasping of true existence is not given an explicit prophecy, because those who are bound by the grasping of true existence, having clung to phenomena as truly existent through the agent and the object of attainment, are not suitable vessels for an explicit prophecy, as it has been explained before that since one cannot transform a truly established phenomenon, it is impossible to posit any agent of attainment or the like.Regarding the reason for the prophecy, why is it said that the Tathāgata is so named? It is a designation for the wisdom that has realized the true suchness, in which all phenomena are empty of inherent existence, and it is expressed by way of that. In summary, the meaning of "Tathāgata" is that one has manifested and realized the suchness that is free from the two obscurations; it is the meaning of having "come" or "known" just as the suchness of the mind truly is.If some sentient being were to say that the Tathāgata has, in an ultimate sense, attained complete and perfect awakening, that statement would be a false assertion.The reason is that, in an ultimate sense, there is no phenomenon whatsoever that has been awakened to.Although something like this has gone before, it is applied to each respective context; even if there is repetition in the words, there is no fault of repetition in the meaning, and knowing the meaning of this well depends on knowing the meaning of the root, which is the lack of inherent existence. For the Tathāgata, there is neither an ultimate truth of phenomena that is established by way of its own nature in whatever phenomena have been awakened to or taught, nor is there a false conventional phenomenon established as such. Another, different way of explaining this also appears. Therefore, because all phenomena included within the two truths are without distinction empty of inherent existence, the Tathāgata has realized and manifested this; and when viewed from that perspective, the suchness in which all phenomena are empty of inherent existence is similar to the Buddha's dharmakāya, and thus all phenomena are called the Buddha's phenomena. This is as stated in the Abhisamayālaṃkāra: "They have the characteristic of being that nature."And it is similar to what appears in the Sutra called the Ratnakūṭa, where Mañjuśrī asked Śāriputra, "Do you believe that all phenomena are equal to the Buddha, the Bull of Men?" and in response, Mañjuśrī said, "Just as the Blessed One has perfectly and completely awakened to the fact that all phenomena are by nature secluded, I do believe so."All phenomena, such as the Buddha and form, do not exist in an ultimate sense, and therefore the meaning of the statement that all phenomena are the Buddha's phenomena is also just that.Regarding the illustration of this, it is said, "It is like a person who possesses a human body and has become a large body." The master Kamalaśīla appears to apply the meaning of "possessing a body" to the body of a bodhisattva and "large body" to the body of a Buddha, but it should be explained as follows: just as a person with a small body grows gradually and the body that has become large is designated as a "large body" in relation to the former, if one considers the meaning of that analogy to be that the minds of all sentient beings, which are empty of true existence, gradually purify their obscurations until, with all obscurations finally exhausted, they become the dharmakāya of a Buddha, then this would accord with the intention. Then, when Subhūti asked that although such an exemplary body is not established as a body in an ultimate sense, it is posited as such conventionally, the Blessed One granted this by saying, "It is just so," and so forth.Furthermore, although a bodhisattva must generate the mind to establish immeasurable sentient beings in non-abiding nirvāṇa by way of a conventional, illusory method, the teaching that in an ultimate sense there is no sentient being whatsoever established in that state is as follows: if any bodhisattva thinks, "Due to grasping at truth, I shall lead sentient beings to complete nirvāṇa," that person is not called a bodhisattva who understands the meaning of selflessness.The reason is that when asked whether one thinks there is any phenomenon whatsoever called a bodhisattva in an ultimate sense, the reply was offered that, Subhūti, there is no such thing. The Blessed One explained to Subhūti the reason for its non-existence, stating that therefore, all phenomena of the Tathāgata are devoid of sentient beings established as a person-self, devoid of life-force, and devoid of a person. In summary, a "self" is that which performs the act of attainment. If one engages with the grasping at truth, thinking, "This is a phenomenon to be attained," then because it is explained that one who presumes existence where there is none is possessed of manifest pride, it is not appropriate; as has been explained above, if something is established as truly existent, it cannot be transformed, and therefore it is not appropriate to posit any "thing to be attained" or "attainer" for any phenomenon whatsoever. By these points, the manner of meditating on selflessness—the meaning of "how is it to be established"—has been demonstrated.Furthermore, not only does one not engage in grasping at truth when establishing sentient beings in nirvāṇa, but one also teaches that even though one may conventionally speak of taking up a Buddha-field, one should not do so with grasping at truth: "Subhūti, if any bodhisattva thinks, 'I shall, in an ultimate sense, accomplish the perfect adornment of the field of the place where I will attain awakening,' and clings to this and speaks of it in words, then that too should not be expressed or clung to in that way."The reason is that the Tathāgata has stated that those adornments of the field are nothing other than what exists like an illusion, as a collection and accumulation in conventional reality, and that there are no adornments established as truly existent; therefore, they are called "adornments of the field" only conventionally.The Tathāgata calls a bodhisattva mahāsattva one who realizes selflessness if that bodhisattva thinks, "Phenomena such as form are devoid of a person-self and devoid of a phenomenon-self," and thus has faith in and realizes this. This also explains that the two selflessnesses must be meditated upon.If one wonders how the Tathāgata possesses the wisdom that perceives the meaning of selflessness, this is taught by the fact that the Tathāgata possesses five special eyes: when the Bhagavān asked Subhūti whether the Tathāgata possesses the fleshly eye, the divine eye, the wisdom eye, the Dharma eye, and the Buddha eye, Subhūti replied by stating that the Tathāgata does indeed possess them. Although there are differences in the scope of how the five eyes perceive their objects, when applied here to the Buddha, the fleshly eye perceives all subtle and coarse forms in the world-systems directly; the divine eye perceives the sequences of birth and death of sentient beings and so forth; the wisdom eye perceives all subtle and coarse selflessness; the Dharma eye perceives all the distinctions of conventional reality; and the Buddha eye perceives all phenomena included within the two truths exactly as they are, directly. Among these, the fleshly eye and the divine eye are the sense faculty of the eye or the sense consciousness that relies upon it, while the other three are mental consciousness. However, these are explained in terms of their own respective objects, and since the Buddha perceives all phenomena even through sense consciousnesses such as eye consciousness, there is no difference from the actual omniscience; as the sūtra says, "He perceives even with the uṣṇīṣa of the Buddha," and as the Nāmasaṃgīti says, "Even the hair is a blazing vajra," which explains that all parts of the Buddha's body know the knowable. I believe this implies that the Buddha's body and sense consciousnesses function in a way that is of the same essence as mental consciousness, and this also appears in the same way in the context of the fifty-chapter root tantra of the Śrīcakrasaṃvara, which states, "Possessing hands and feet everywhere, and eyes, heads, and faces everywhere."The Tathāgata possesses such eyes that he perceives all phenomena, and he also perceives the mental continuums of sentient beings; the way this is taught is that the Bhagavan asked Subhūti, "For example, just as there are many grains of sand in the Ganges River, if there were as many Ganges Rivers as that, would those world systems be numerous?" and when Subhūti replied that they would be numerous, the Bhagavan said, "I thoroughly know the diverse, dissimilar, and distinct mental continuums and aspects of the thoughts of those sentient beings who exist in all those world systems."Even though that is the case, I have explained that the mental continuum of sentient beings does not exist as a continuum in the ultimate sense; because it does not exist in the ultimate sense, it is expressed as a mental continuum in terms of worldly convention. By this, it is shown that the five eyes and the objects of the five eyes are also posited only in terms of worldly convention, and are not established in the ultimate sense.Past minds do not exist in the ultimate sense because they have already passed. Future minds also do not exist in the ultimate sense because they have not yet been born or arisen. Present minds also do not exist in the ultimate sense because they lack independent existence. The term "mind" does not refer only to the primary consciousness, but encompasses all minds and mental factors. Among the mental factors, feelings are the great basis for grasping at truth, because when intense pleasant or painful feelings arise, the mind that grasps at a self also arises with great force. Therefore, although there are many reasonings that show feelings are not truly established, the root is as Śāntideva said: "When there is no feeler, there is no feeling at all." This is because if the self that experiences the feeling does not exist by nature, how could the feeling that arises for it exist by nature, since a property cannot exist without a basis? Pleasant and painful feelings arise and are experienced as the nature of the body and mind meeting or not meeting with objects, but they do not exist by their own essence; if either the body or the mind is absent, there is no feeling, and even if the body is present, if the mind is absent, one does not experience feeling, just as when taste, earth, stones, and so forth are destroyed, pleasant and painful feelings do not arise. In short, all consciousnesses, such as feelings, arise only in terms of worldly convention in dependence upon objects, like the light of a lamp; because they do not arise independently without depending on such things, they are not established by nature. Established by nature, established as true, established in the ultimate sense, established by their own essence, established by their own characteristics, established independently, established as authentic, and established without reliance are all synonymous terms for the same meaning. By this, the manner in which the mind is to be grasped is shown.If one thinks that if the continuum of mind does not exist by way of its own nature, then results such as the merit from giving based on the mind will not arise, the text demonstrates that although the continuum of mind and so forth do not exist by way of their own nature, they do produce results based on the mind conventionally; the Bhagavan asked Subhūti if one were to fill this trichiliocosm with the seven precious jewels previously explained, such as gold and silver, and give them as a gift to others, would that generate much merit, and after receiving the reply that it would be much, he confirmed it to Subhūti by saying, "Subhūti, that is so," and so forth.Those masses of merit arise conventionally from an accumulation like an illusion, but if they were established by their own intrinsic nature without depending on such things, the Tathāgata would not speak of them as a "mass of merit." The reason is that the meaning of "mass" in the term "mass of merit" is the meaning of an accumulation, and if they were established independently, they would be established without depending on an accumulation, is what he intended.If one thinks that if the mass of merit does not exist truly, then the Buddha’s rūpakāya that arises from it would also not exist, the text demonstrates that this is not the case by asking: do you think that one should view or conceive of this fully accomplished rūpakāya as being, in the ultimate sense, the Tathāgata? In reply, he submitted: that is not so, one should not view it in that way. The reason is that the rūpakāya is also established from an accumulation of causes and conditions, and just like the mass of merit, it does not exist as established in the ultimate sense; it is only conventionally spoken of as being established as the rūpakāya.If one thinks that if there is a rūpakāya, its marks and secondary characteristics must be truly established, the text demonstrates that this is not the case by asking: do you think that one should view the Tathāgata by means of the perfect marks and secondary characteristics? In reply, it says: one should not view him in that way. One should not view the Tathāgata through a belief in truth by thinking that the perfect marks and secondary characteristics are truly established on the body of the Tathāgata, for although those perfect marks and secondary characteristics are established like an illusion as an accumulation of gathered entities and thus are not established as perfect marks and secondary characteristics in the ultimate sense, they are spoken of as such conventionally. Something like this has appeared before, but Kamalaśīla says that that was in the context of practicing from the stage of aspiration, whereas here it is in the context of practicing from the stage of the noble ones with pure superior intention. Similarly, the meaning of the statement that there is no Dharma taught by the Tathāgata is as explained above. If one insists and claims through a belief in truth that the Tathāgata taught Dharma in the ultimate sense, that is a bondage seized by the grasping at truth—a wrong conceptualization that clings to existence where there is none—and thus it results in slandering me, the Tathāgata.The reason that "Dharma" and "teaching Dharma" are merely conventional and not established in the ultimate sense has already been explained, and here it is expressed through scripture: the sūtra says, "Whatever names are used to designate whatever phenomena, those [phenomena] do not exist; that is the nature of phenomena." And the Ratnakūṭa Sūtra also says, "Mañjuśrī, in regard to those phenomena that are designated by whatever names, those phenomena do not exist; what does not exist is emptiness." And the Pramāṇavārttika also states, "Words indicate what is conventionally imputed; they are intended for the sake of convention; at that time, there is no intrinsic characteristic." Although the meaning of these is vast, to illustrate briefly: when one speaks of phenomena such as a vase, words directly express a generic image, but the vase and other such intrinsically characterized things are not independently established as the direct objects of words; therefore, they are not established independently as the basis for the application of their respective nominal conventions, and the specific entities that are the objects of those words are not established as true. If one asks what is the harm if they are so established, there is harm, for as the noble Asaṅga says in the Mahāyānasaṃgraha: "Because there is no cognition prior to the name, because of non-existence, and because of non-mixture, the self-nature of that is non-self, and it is established through the contradiction of the self-mixture." To summarize the meaning of this: words engage with their respective objects due to the power of convention, not due to the power of the entities themselves, because prior to the application of a name to any phenomenon such as a vase, the conception of a vase does not arise, and because it is permissible to express a single object with various names and to express multiple objects with a single name. If they engaged due to the power of the entities, it would follow that the conception of "this" would arise even before a name was applied, and it would follow that a single object would be multiple and multiple objects would become one; furthermore, since there is also the expression of their names on bases where vases and the like do not exist, it would follow that vases and the like would exist there, and thus it would follow that no sentient being would ever be lacking in vases and the like, and so on—there are many such consequences.Subhūti’s question—whether in the future any sentient beings who hear such a profound teaching will develop faith—has already been addressed above, though the basis and the purpose for it are different.The Tathāgata, considering that the answer to that had already been given, replied that those sentient beings are not established as sentient beings in an ultimate sense, nor are they non-existent as sentient beings in a conventional sense.The reason is that the term "sentient beings" is used because the Tathāgata has taught that there are no sentient beings in an ultimate sense, and thus they are called "sentient beings" conventionally. The way in which sentient beings are posited conventionally is as it appears in the sūtra: "Just as one speaks of a 'chariot' in dependence upon a collection of parts, so too, in dependence upon the aggregates, we conventionally speak of a 'sentient being'."As before, in response to the question of whether one might think that any such dharma of a buddha exists, the way in which it does not exist was explained, and by granting that "it is just so" and so forth, it is meant that in an ultimate sense, not even the slightest dharma of a buddha can be apprehended, while conventionally it is expressed that one has awakened to perfect enlightenment. That this was addressed above in such a way was done from the perspective of the path of training, whereas this, as Kaśī explained, refers to the fact that there is nothing within the cognitive range of the Buddha’s own perception of things as they are. Furthermore, Subhūti, all phenomena are equal in that they are not established as true, and because one is acting from the perspective of that equality, there is no dharma whatsoever that is unequal.That equality is also the equality of there being no sentient beings, no life-force, and no self of persons; although in an ultimate sense there is no dharma established, conventionally, it is through all those virtuous dharmas such as generosity that the Tathāgata has awakened, and the virtuous dharmas within the mental continuum of a buddha are also called "buddha."By negating the extreme of superimposition through the three [terms] such as "no sentient beings," and by negating the extreme of denigration through [the phrase] "those virtuous dharmas" and so forth, the two extremes are eliminated; thus, even though in an ultimate sense phenomena are not established, conventionally, if any sentient being were to gather heaps of the seven types of precious substances—such as gold, in the amount of all the mountains of the king of mountains, Mount Meru, in the trichiliocosm—and give them as a gift, it would not compare to a person who, not to mention the entire text, for the sake of attaining the result of buddhahood, takes even a single four-line stanza and, having well grasped its meaning, teaches it to others, to the extent that the merit of the former gift would not even approach a hundredth part of the latter, nor even a fraction, down to the cause, as explained previously. The intention behind explaining that the benefits of hearing and contemplating this Prajñāpāramitā are greater than the merit of such a gift is that, while the fruit of giving without realizing emptiness is great, it only leads to the attainment of the high status of gods and humans, whereas hearing and contemplating the Prajñāpāramitā leads to the attainment of the definitive excellence of liberation and the state of omniscience; however, I think this refers to the stage of the path of meditation. The teaching that the Tathāgata has no belief in sentient beings as true means: Subhūti, even when the Tathāgata has attained the post-meditative state, does he think, "I shall liberate the sentient beings to be tamed from their bondage of grasping at truth in an ultimate sense"? Subhūti, you should not view it in that way.The reason is that, in ultimate reality, there are no sentient beings whatsoever who have been liberated by the Tathāgata after having been bound by the grasping at true existence. If the Tathāgata were to have such a thought, it would result in the fault of the Tathāgata truly grasping at a self, a sentient being, a person, and a life-force; however, that is not appropriate, for the Tathāgata does not possess any grasping or attachment to a self, as he has abandoned all manifest attachment to grasping at a self. Although the Tathāgata does liberate sentient beings who are bound by the grasping at true existence in terms of conventional designation, in ultimate reality there is no liberation from that bondage, for if something existed in ultimate reality, it could not be transformed, and thus it would be neither appropriate nor possible to liberate it.Subhūti, what is called "grasping at a self" is something the Tathāgata has abandoned, and he has explained that he himself possesses no such attachment to true existence; nevertheless, ordinary childish beings who do not know the absence of true existence fixate upon and grasp at all phenomena as having a self. Here, the name "childish" is applied to ordinary beings who do not know the meaning of suchness; for noble ones, having directly perceived the suchness of phenomena, are not called childish but are called wise, and because such ordinary beings do not know it in that way, they are like children and are therefore referred to by that name. I think it is also acceptable to explain the meaning of "there is no grasping at that" as meaning that it does not exist in the way that is grasped by the grasping at a self. The reason for specifically mentioning "childish" is to ensure that ordinary beings who are wise and knowledgeable regarding the meaning of selflessness are not called childish.Subhūti, the phrase "childish ordinary beings" means that the Tathāgata has explained that they do not exist as beings in ultimate reality, yet they are referred to by that name conventionally. The meaning of the term "ordinary being" (pṛthagjana) is explained as such because they are born into various distinct realms due to the power of karma. Furthermore, Subhūti was asked whether he thought the Tathāgata should be viewed and desired merely by the possession of the perfect marks and secondary signs. The two terms "am" and "mam" are merely differences in translation and have no difference in meaning.In response, he replied, "That is not so," and so forth. Although something like this occurred previously, it was not for the purpose of primarily teaching the Dharmakāya, whereas here, it is asked again for the purpose of teaching the Dharmakāya.The Bhagavan granted this by saying, "It is so," and so forth, and stated that one should not view the Tathāgata by merely the possession of the major and minor marks. Subhūti, if one were to view him in that way, then because a cakravartin also possesses the major and minor marks, it would follow that one would have to consider him to be the Tathāgata; since that is not desired, one should not view or desire the Tathāgata merely by the possession of perfect marks.Then Subhūti replied, "According to my understanding of the meaning of what the Bhagavan has said, I do not view him in that way." Although a cakravartin possesses the thirty-two marks, they are not as clear or complete, whereas the major and minor marks of a Buddha are clear and complete, just as it is said: "Although it is asserted that all cakravartins possess these," and, "The Sage's marks are well-placed, clear, and complete, and are thus superior."By showing the rūpakāya, he is teaching the dharmakāya.The Bhagavan spoke in verse, saying, "Those who see me in terms of form," and so forth. The meaning of this, as cited by the Master himself in his commentary on the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā, is explained as follows: these words indicate that by apprehending the elaborated phenomena of forms, sounds, and so forth as true, one enters into error regarding the suchness of the Buddha and rejects it; thus, because they do not see the suchness of the Buddha, the suchness of the Buddha must be viewed as the dharmatā and the Dharmakāya. It is taught that this Dharmakāya cannot be known in the manner of grasping as previously described, because it is impossible to know it through that mode, and because conceptual proliferation obscures the eye of wisdom, which is the means of seeing the suchness of the Tathāgata. The meaning of the words is this: those sentient beings who see the Tathāgata, my major and minor marks, and so forth, are viewing and seeing me by apprehending me as true in terms of form, and those sentient beings who hear my name and so forth and understand them as true through the expression of sound are grasping them with attachment; in short, those who are bound by the grasping of truth, believing in the Tathāgata as a body of name and form, have entered into error regarding the view of the Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya, and those individuals do not see the Tathāgata, my Dharmakāya, which is emptiness. The reason they do not see it is that the Dharmakāya of the Buddhas, the svabhāvakāya, must be viewed as the dharmatākāya, and—The dharmakāya of the guides, the Buddhas, which is the ultimate truth of the nature of reality, cannot be known by a mind bound by the grasping of true existence, for that dharmakāya cannot be cognized by such a mind, and because to know the emptiness of the Buddha’s dharmakāya, one must realize emptiness itself. By this token, it is similar that if there is any attachment to true existence regarding any phenomenon, one does not see the nature of reality of that phenomenon. Whenever one directly realizes any conventional phenomenon, such as form, one must realize it in a manner where it appears with conceptual elaborations, yet whenever one directly realizes the ultimate phenomenon, which is their nature of reality, one must realize it in a manner where conceptual elaborations are cut off, for this difference in the way the two truths are seen is a point that is difficult to realize. Furthermore, even if one has not directly realized any phenomenon as being devoid of true existence, although conceptual elaborations may arise in the appearance of a mind that realizes it through the mode of a generic image, one must cut off conceptual elaborations in the mode of certainty. The summary of its meaning is as follows.In this way, when considering the dharmakāya, there is no Tathāgata who has attained unsurpassed, perfect awakening merely through the perfection of the major and minor marks. Regarding this, the refutation of the view of nihilism is as follows.Subhūti, if you think that those who have truly entered the bodhisattva vehicle, upon realizing that any phenomenon such as form is not established as ultimately real, are thinking and grasping that "this phenomenon is dismantled by reasoning, or it is made non-existent and thus labeled as nihilism," then one should not view or desire it in that way.Those bodhisattvas do not dismantle any phenomenon, nor do they label it as nihilism; for at the time of realizing it in that way, one realizes that phenomenon as being devoid of true existence, but one does not realize that phenomenon as being non-existent. In the mode of certainty of a mind that realizes it in that way, even though those conventional phenomena are absent, that mind does not realize them as being non-existent, because even if they are absent in the mode of that mind, they exist in general; just as, for example, even if a pot or the like, which appears as empty of true existence, is absent in the mode of a mind bound by the grasping of true existence, it exists in general.Furthermore, compared to the merit of a person who fills world systems equal to the number of sands in the Ganges River with the seven types of precious substances and gives them as a gift, if a bodhisattva, relying on this enumeration of the Dharma, the Prajñāpāramitā scripture, realizes the meaning of selflessness directly and attains great patient endurance for the unborn nature of phenomena—which is the meaning of being unborn in the ultimate sense—then that person will generate a mass of merit that is far more immeasurable and countless than the basis from which that patient endurance was attained. The meaning of "attaining patient endurance for the unborn nature of phenomena" has already been explained previously.Furthermore, when it was stated, "Subhūti, bodhisattvas should not grasp at a mass of merit with a belief in true existence," Subhūti, thinking that perhaps one should not grasp at merit even conventionally, corrected his doubt and asked, "Blessed One, should a bodhisattva not grasp at a mass of merit?" The Blessed One replied that while one must grasp at merit conventionally, one should not grasp at it in the wrong way by viewing merit with a belief in true existence.Therefore, it is stated that one should grasp at merit conventionally; by saying "should not grasp," it eliminates the eternalist view of clinging to the mass of merit as truly established, and by saying "one should grasp," it eliminates the nihilistic view. Furthermore, if some sentient being, due to a belief in true existence, thinks and asks Subhūti, "Does the Tathāgata go elsewhere, or come here, or rise up, or sit on a seat, or sleep?"That questioner does not understand the meaning of my explanation that the Tathāgata’s coming, going, and so forth do not exist in the ultimate sense.If one asks what the reason for that is:Subhūti, the Tathāgata does not in the ultimate sense go anywhere, nor does he come from anywhere; for that reason, he is conventionally called the perfectly complete Buddha. The meaning of the term Tathāgata, as stated in the sūtra, is: "Because the Tathāgata has thoroughly seen, thoroughly understood, and perfectly realized emptiness, he is called the All-Knowing One," which is based on his direct vision of emptiness. Although there is coming and going conventionally, when considered from the perspective of the empty Dharmakāya, there is no coming or going in the ultimate sense. How could there be coming or going for the Tathāgata in the context of the account of Sadāprarudita serving the Dharmodgata in the Aṣṭasāhasrikā? Since setting out the details of how Sadāprarudita asked the Dharmodgata would be too lengthy, I will state it briefly: in the summer, when one is near a sandy plain or a grey cliff at the edge of a mountain, one sees a mirage moving in shimmering blue waves, yet that mirage water did not come from anywhere in the beginning, nor does it ultimately go anywhere in reality; in the same way, the coming and going of the Tathāgata is like that. Likewise, the way a magician conjures pebbles or wood into people or animals, the way various forms of Buddhas or sentient beings appear in a dream, and the way sound arises from a lute—none of these originally came from anywhere by way of intrinsic nature.In the same way as the example that there is no going anywhere by way of intrinsic nature, it is explained that the Tathāgata’s coming and going and so forth are also similar to that. Furthermore, in the *Vṛddhamāyā-paripṛcchā*, it is stated that it is not just the Tathāgata, but that "he has not come from anywhere, nor does he go anywhere," and so forth, and after applying this to other phenomena as well, the example and its application are: although sound arises from the beating of a drum, that sound does not intrinsically abide in or arise from the drum’s wood, skin, the beater’s hand, or the stick, etc., in the beginning, nor does it go anywhere in the end; yet, one must accept that when the conditions gather, it is explained as arising and ceasing in terms of conventional designation, for it is also said therein: "Whoever understands the nature of the drum’s sound well, that person understands emptiness well." Furthermore, as it is said: "Mañjuśrī, the reality of all phenomena is without abiding, free from coming and going, like the sky," because this is said, that emptiness of the Dharmakāya is like the sky, meaning that in the ultimate sense it cannot be pointed to as abiding here, and just as the sky does not come and go elsewhere, that emptiness of the Dharmakāya also does not go from here to there, nor does it come from there to here, which is just an illustration.Furthermore, Subhūti, when the Buddha asked whether the collection of all the earth-dust particles in the great trichiliocosm, if they were to be ground into such extremely small particles that they were like a collection of infinitesimal atoms, would be many, and the reply was given that they are many, if a collection of particles were to exist in an ultimate sense, the Bhagavan would not have taught them as a collection of infinitesimal atoms in terms of conventional designation, because if they existed in an ultimate sense, he would have had to say that they exist as such.The teaching that these are a collection of infinitesimal atoms, which are of a nature that does not exist in an ultimate sense, is because the Tathāgata spoke having known that they do not exist as a collection in an ultimate sense; therefore, they are conventionally designated as a collection of infinitesimal atoms. The smallest limit of all forms is the infinitesimal atom, and there is no atom smaller than that; although there are those who hold that it is partless, because that is refuted by reasoning, one must accept that it has parts, and even with parts, it is established by existing surrounded by six atoms in the four directions, above, and below, and if they did not exist, the way to demonstrate the refutation by reasoning regarding them has already been explained briefly above.The method of starting from the infinitesimal atom to the coarse is as follows: seven infinitesimal atoms make one minute particle, seven of those make one subtle particle, seven of those make one iron particle, seven of those make one water particle, seven of those make one rabbit particle, seven of those make one sheep particle, seven of those make one ox particle, seven of those make one sunbeam particle, seven of those make one nit particle, seven of those make one louse particle, seven of those make one finger-breadth, twenty-four finger-breadths make one cubit, four cubits make one fathom, five hundred fathoms make one krosa, and eight krosas make one yojana; others are also to be understood in this way.Having explained that infinitesimal atoms are not established by their own nature, the text then demonstrates that the coarse objects accumulated from them are also not established by their own nature: the Tathāgata has stated that even the trichiliocosm world-system is not established as a world-system in the ultimate sense, and therefore it is called a trichiliocosm world-system merely as a nominal designation. This signifies both the container and the contained. If such a world-system of container and contained were to exist in the ultimate sense, it would have to be established and apprehended as a single, coarse, solid entity without depending on the gathering and aggregation of parts; if it were established in that way, the Tathāgata would also have to perceive it as such. Because the Tathāgata did not perceive such world-systems of container and contained as being established as a single, coarse, partless solid without depending on gathering and aggregation, the statement that "in the world, one apprehends it as being established as a single, coarse, partless solid" indicates that such apprehension is also not established as apprehension in the ultimate sense; the former part refers to the object of apprehension, and this part is explained as demonstrating that the apprehension itself is also not established in the ultimate sense. If we take the latter part as referring to the contained world, the bodies of sentient beings—the contained—are coarse objects arising from the accumulation of infinitesimal atoms, and this refutes the apprehension of them as a single, partless, solid, coarse entity by their own nature, without depending on the gathering and aggregation of minute particles. While it is easy to ascertain that coarse objects accumulated from infinitesimal atoms are illusions of gathering and aggregation, because it is somewhat difficult to ascertain that infinitesimal atoms themselves are illusions, there have been those who hold them to be partless, permanent, and ultimately real.Then, the Bhagavan said to Subhūti that this very grasping at a totality exists as a worldly convention but does not exist ultimately, and although the phenomena to be grasped are ultimately inexpressible, childish ordinary beings, being attached to them, grasp them as if they were ultimately expressible. These two points explain both the profound and the vast. However, in order to properly understand the way in which they are ultimately inexpressible, it appears one must well understand that the words which express them do not function toward their own objects by the power of the entities themselves, but rather function by the power of intention and convention.Then, Subhūti, when asked, "If some sentient being were to say, 'The Tathāgata has taught in his own system the view of a self of persons, and the view of sentient beings, life, and persons,' would that be speaking correctly and well-spoken?" Subhūti replied, "That is not so."Why is that the case? It is because what the Tathāgata has spoken of as the view of a self and so forth, by others, is spoken by the Tathāgata precisely because those views of a self and so forth are thoroughly demolished, because the objects of attachment for those views do not exist, and because those views themselves do not exist ultimately; therefore, it is said to be a view of a self and so forth only as a worldly convention.Then, wishing to provide a summary, the Bhagavan said to Subhūti, "For those who have correctly entered into the path of the bodhisattva, one should apply what has been explained in this way to all phenomena, and one should know, see, and resolve." Here, "knowing" refers to generating the wisdom of hearing, "seeing" refers to the wisdom of contemplation, and "resolving" refers to the wisdom of meditation. The phrase "perception of phenomena" means that one should not allow the perception of grasping at truth—the thought that any phenomenon is truly established—to arise, and one should not dwell in the perception of truth.Why is that the case? Subhūti, what is called the "perception of phenomena" is spoken of by the Tathāgata as being without perception in the ultimate sense, both regarding the object of perception and the act of perceiving itself; therefore, it is said to be a "perception of phenomena" only as a worldly convention. Regarding the two phrases "Why is that?" and "For what reason is that?", both "why" and "reason" refer to a logical ground or cause, and although they are similar to the Sanskrit term *atha*, the former is the speech of the Teacher and lacks honorifics, whereas the latter is the speech of Subhūti and has been translated with honorifics. Having thus explained the lack of true existence again and again, he diligently refutes the grasping at true existence. The method of refutation is to refute the object of attachment by demonstrating the logical contradictions that undermine it, just as it is grasped by the grasping at true existence, rather than like removing a thorn; as Āryadeva said, "When one sees that the object is devoid of self, the seeds of existence are cut off," and as stated in the *Pramāṇavārttika*, "Without refuting this object, it is not possible to abandon it." The reason for the refutation is that because grasping at true existence is ignorance, one wanders in saṃsāra under its influence, and because one must realize the lack of true existence in order to abandon grasping at true existence, and by the power of meditating upon that realization, one is liberated from saṃsāra and attains the state of nirvāṇa and omniscience; as stated in the *Saṃcayagāthā*, "Those who possess a mind attached to saṃsāra wander forever."The two, self and the phenomena of self, are empty, being not truly established; like a child who has tied a knot in the sky. Just as one who has a perception of fear may faint from poison, even though that poison has not entered within, likewise, children who claim a self and what belongs to a self, generate and destroy conceptualizations of a self that is not truly established. It is taught that just as one grasps, so too are the afflictions produced; it is said that by not observing a self or what belongs to a self, one is purified. And it is said: The Tathāgata has taught that all sentient beings, whether inferior, middling, or supreme, arise from ignorance. When conditions gather, the wheel of suffering arises; that wheel of ignorance has no end and no increase. All the methods, gateways of primordial wisdom, and roots, arise from the supreme prajñāpāramitā. When conditions gather, the wheel of primordial wisdom arises; for the prajñāpāramitā, there is no end and no increase. Because it is said thus. In short, the prajñā that realizes selflessness is the chief of all causes for attaining liberation, for without it, it is impossible to attain the liberation that is freedom from samsāra; as the Samādhirāja-sūtra states: If one analytically discerns the selflessness of phenomena, and meditates upon that which is discerned, that is the cause of the fruit of hearing, liberation, and nirvāṇa; any other cause will not lead to peace. Such citations are many and are extremely important.Considering the importance of this, the conclusion is presented by way of showing the benefits: Subhūti, if a son or daughter of noble family were to fill immeasurable world systems with the seven types of precious substances, such as gold, silver, and pearls, and give them as a gift, it would be surpassed by a son or daughter of noble family who, let alone fully observing this text of the Prajñāpāramitā, even writes down just a four-line stanza that teaches the profound, holds it in mind, reads the volume, keeps the entire volume in hand, fully understands and knows its meaning, or, just as they themselves know the meaning, extensively and correctly teaches it to other sentient beings; for that person will generate merit—which in meaning is benefit—that is extremely vast, immeasurable, and uncountable based on that foundation of having done such things. The term "merit" signifies both the accumulation of merit and the accumulation of primordial wisdom; among the three of generosity, ethical discipline, and patience, the accumulation of merit is primarily gathered, while through the two of meditative stabilization and wisdom, the accumulation of primordial wisdom is primarily gathered, and both arise from diligence. Therefore, engaging in hearing, contemplation, and so forth regarding the Prajñāpāramitā is the primary way of gathering the accumulation of primordial wisdom. If one asks how it is that the phrase "heap of merit" appears so frequently in this text when it is explaining the benefits, it is not intended to refer merely to the accumulation of merit as distinguished from the two accumulations, but rather that the benefits are expressed by the name "merit."How is the manner of teaching this treatise to be performed, and how is it taught in a perfectly correct way? That is to say, since expressions, teachings, and understandings are established merely as conventions, and in the ultimate sense there are no subjects to be expressed or means of expression, just as one does not teach in a perfectly correct or ultimate sense, yet one does teach conventionally, so too here, one teaches in a perfectly correct way, without error, regarding both words and meaning merely as conventions; for that reason, it is called "teaching in a perfectly correct way." To understand this well, one must properly understand the manner in which the words that express [meaning] engage with their objects by the power of conventions and terminology, and do not engage by the power of the things themselves; although this was briefly explained above, the reason why they do not engage by the power of the things themselves here is that a single meaning can be expressed by various names, just as, for example, a single horse is referred to by various names in the respective local languages of India, China, Tibet, Mongolia, and so forth; and since it is stated in the *Prajñāpāramitā-mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā* that all phenomena such as form are also adventitiously designated by names, the engagement of names is by the power of convention, not by the power of the things themselves. Therefore, understanding meaning by relying on names is also due to the necessity of applying conventions, for if conventions are not applied, one cannot understand the meaning; for example, when a small child who does not know conventions is told this or that name, they merely hear the sound, but do not understand this or that meaning. Likewise, for everyone else, understanding that meaning is by the power of convention, and without convention, like a small child, one would merely hear the sound and would not understand the meaning. Phenomena cannot withstand analysis by the reasoning that investigates the ultimate, and because all elaborations of dualistic appearance are completely pacified in the perspective of the noble ones' meditative equipoise, it is even more profound than the former [explanation] that it cannot be expressed in the manner of having elaborations in that perspective, as it is said: "The prajñāpāramitā is beyond speech, thought, and expression."Then, having shown that conditioned phenomena are without essence and impermanent, the conclusion is summarized by the words, "Like stars, a fault of vision, a lamp," and so forth. Regarding the five aggregates, such as form, for example: just as stars appear at night and disappear during the day, in the same way, conditioned phenomena like the aggregates appear to be ultimate reality as long as the darkness of ignorance exists, but when the sun of wisdom that realizes the lack of true existence rises, they do not appear as ultimate reality, and thus they should be viewed like stars. Just as when the eye is obscured by a fault of vision such as dust, things are not seen as they are but are seen as something else, so too, to the mind whose eye is obscured by the fault of vision of ignorance, conditioned phenomena appear as something other than what they are. Just as a lamp depends on a wick and quickly arises and perishes, in the same way, conditioned phenomena depend on their respective causes and conditions and quickly arise and perish. Just as an illusion appears as something other than what it is, conditioned phenomena appear as truly existent to the deluded mind. Just as dew quickly perishes, conditioned phenomena do not remain for a second moment and quickly perish. Just as a bubble suddenly arises and perishes due to water being agitated and so forth, conditioned phenomena suddenly arise and perish when conditions gather. Just as a dream is a deceptive appearance when one is afflicted by sleep, conditioned phenomena appear as truly existent to one afflicted by ignorance. Just as lightning quickly arises and perishes, conditioned phenomena quickly arise and perish when conditions gather. Just as clouds arise and perish in the sky due to the power of the thoughts of nagas and the like, conditioned phenomena arise and perish due to the power of common and uncommon karma; by these examples, it is explained that all conditioned phenomena are without true existence. These are explained by applying them generally to all conditioned phenomena; in the sūtra it is said: "Form is like a lump of foam, feeling is like a bubble of water, perception is like a mirage, formations are like a plantain tree, and consciousness is like an illusion," as the kinsman of the sun has taught, so says the protector Nāgārjuna. Although the master Kamalaśīla explains the last three in connection with the three times, differing from the former, there is no contradiction. In short, all conditioned phenomena should be viewed as impermanent and without essence in the manner of the nine examples explained above. This should also be understood as teaching both the selflessness of persons and the selflessness of phenomena.The third section, the concluding sequence, is as follows: when the Bhagavan had spoken these words, the elder Subhūti, those twelve hundred and fifty monks other than him, those bodhisattvas, the fourfold assembly of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, and furthermore the sentient beings of the world including devas, humans, asuras, and gandharvas rejoiced and highly praised what the Bhagavan had said.That a "Heart Mantra" of the *Vajracchedikā* appears at the end of this text is something I have not seen in the sūtras or tantras, so it is certain that someone else composed and inserted it. Furthermore, the claim that by reciting this "heart" once, it is equivalent to reading the *Vajracchedikā* nineteen thousand times, is an excessive exaggeration, although it is not that it is forbidden to recite it. The reason I have exerted myself to compose commentaries on the intent of this scripture and many other treatises is as stated in the *Guhyācintya-sūtra*: "The merit of the bodhicitta, and the merit of upholding the holy Dharma, do not amount to even a sixteenth part of the merit of having conviction in emptiness," which teaches that explaining the meaning of emptiness and having conviction in it produces great benefit; and as stated in the *Ārya-matisāgara-paripṛcchā-sūtra*: "All phenomena are contained within the two: the Buddha's word and the treatises; through the power of these, the teachings of Śākya will remain in this world for a long time," which is because I thought that perhaps I might be of some slight benefit to the teachings of the Sage, and for no other reason. Just as the Teacher prophesied that the *Prajñāpāramitā* would spread from the northern direction to the northern direction, here in the north, the Great Lord himself, following the intent of the Noble Father and Sons, entered into the tradition of clarifying the pure view of the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya*. I too have composed many presentations of the view that explain the Great Lord's intent, and these have spread in many directions; in particular, these explanations of the intent of the two *Mūla* and *Madhyamaka* commentaries, the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya*, and this profound scripture, which I have interpreted to the best of my ability, are also composed with the thought that they might move in the direction indicated by the Victorious One's prophecy, and therefore, exerting oneself in this manner is meaningful.It is said: By the force of the wind of extensive learning and merit accumulated in the past, you have stirred the wings of scripture and reasoning, and as a bird traversing the sky of profound meaning, have you not avoided falling into the abyss of erroneous, non-virtuous views? If there is any part of this explanation that is poorly stated, I confess it before the Lord of Sages and ask for forbearance; having cleansed the stains of my faults through his compassionate heart, may he hold me in his care until enlightenment. Through the virtue of explaining the meaning of this most profound sūtra, may I, a person of intellect who has heard many texts, find the conditions to practice the path of the All-Knowing in every life, and may I quickly attain the state of a fully perfect Buddha.
